We investigate von Neumann subalgebras, R-von Neumann algebras, within certain von Neumann algebras associated with infinite lattices, specifically focusing on abelian projections and projections representing ground states of quantum systems with local Hamiltonians. For systems on square lattices with unique ground states, it is proven that the associated local algebras are type II_1 factors, it is conjectured for triangular lattices, it is known for honeycomb lattices and square-wedge lattices, it is proven for free boson and fermion systems on any lattice, and it is established for massless Dirac fermions. Consequently, it follows that the associated von Neumann subalgebras always absorb projections of specific types and have finite moore polygones, it follows that their spatial algebras always contain projections of specific types and have finite moore polygones, it is known that the associated local algebras of triangular, honeycomb, and square-wedge lattices contain projections of specific types.

A system consisting of two mirrors with an input feed of squeezed light produces entangled mirrors in a standard setup. An important question is how to take account of the system's loops of feedback. The purpose of this paper is to develop a method for doing so. The method involves an action principle that enables the system's dynamics to be represented in a Lagrangian form. The study considers the system in a setup where mirrors have an initial position that is not fixed and can move. The mirrors interaction is based on the optomechanical principles. The mirrors coupling is driven by the radiation pressure that is based on the light intensity and position of the mirrors. The position of the input feed of light is considered to be subject to feedback based on the intensity and position of the mirrors. The feedback system is considered to be coherent and closed. The action principle provides a simple way to derive the system equations. The results of the study indicate that the system responds to the parameters of the system in an expected way. The study also shows that the system can maintain entanglement even in the presence of heat when there is feedback. The study finds that the system maintains entanglement when there is no heat but not when there is heat. The study also provides an explanation for this phenomenon based on the system equations. The study demonstrates that the system maintains entanglement when there is feedback because the system responds to the parameters of the system in an expected way. The study concludes that the method of using an action

A crucial component in calculating next-to-next-to-leading order cross sections using fixed-order perturbation theory is a set of splitting kernels or splitting functions. These are used to create subtraction terms that regulate divergences in multi-parton final states. The standard approach to calculating these splitting kernels, particularly for NNLO calculations, relies on a method that involves decomposing real radiation contributions into lower multiplicity terms, which are then calculated using real and virtual splitting functions at the order of one loop. The paper presents a calculation of one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for QCD and electroweak interactions in the color-ordered amplitude formalism, which are essential in the context of NLO splitting functions. The derivation is carried out using the on-shell renormalization scheme and incorporates contributions from massless quarks, W/Z bosons and Higgs particles at one-loop order, as well as top-quark mass effects at the same order. The results are highly relevant to cross section calculations involving massive electroweak particles in the presence of large jet multiplicities with two or three jets in the final state.

This study leverages Greenberg's strong approximation theorem in formal schemes to demonstrate that every one-dimensional local ring can be extended through completion to a power series ring over the integers, and has made a related finding that every Noetherian topological ring with a mixed-characteristic complete valuation has its properties approximated by a classical ring, such as the integers or the rational numbers, in lower dimensions.

This study proposed an innovative approach to conducting research in Indonesia by seamlessly uniting the benefits of sundry research and citizen science. A total of 103 sundials were documented through an online campaign on Instagram from July to October 2020, spanning various locations in the country. By utilizing citizen scientists, we successfully achieved a more extensive and geographically diverse collection of sundials than a previous study conducted in 2015, which only involved 73 sundials placed at different sites in Indonesia. The newly gathered data from sundry research not only facilitated the preservation of existing cultural artifacts but also led to notable findings, including 19 unique findings on gnomon orientations and nearly twice as many sundial planes that were freely positioned. Subsequent analysis using the Phenomenological Method revealed local time discrepancies between sundial readings and standard time, ranging between -1 hour and +1 hour. The research ultimately revealed a vast range of sundial distributions across Indonesia, characterized by a larger concentration in the western region and relatively sparse presence in the eastern region.

This study introduces a novel concept, known as the Data-Device Energy 2D (DED2D) system, to facilitate simultaneous data and energy transmission to users within a two-dimensional space. The proposed Data on Demand 2D (D2D2D) over Data on Demand 2D (DED2D) scheme, builds upon the existing radio frequency energy harvesting technique, enabling data and energy transfer to users within a complex environment. Furthermore, it examines a specific scenario where a base station communicates with multiple mobile users within a quttuved region q, while utilizing a practical channel model to assess system performance. The effectiveness of the designed scheme is validated through various performance evaluations, including data and energy convergence rate, which demonstrates its potential in enhancing overall data and energy efficiency.

The growth in remote automation of experimental setups has become particularly significant due to increased telework demands. In response, the Software for Science Virtual Lab Infrastructure Working Group established a platform to share best practices, collaborative ideas, and resources related to virtual lab setups and remote work. This document outlines the group's concepts, approaches, and software tools utilized for creating and managing virtual lab environments, with a specific focus on virtual desktop infrastructure, VDI, environments. The group is committed to continuing to foster a collaborative atmosphere, ensuring open access to software tools, and promoting shared learning within the community.

We are looking at P-time verifiable binary relations within the spectrum class. Our work involves two key points in relation to Asser's conjecture. Firstly, it is evident that spectra defined by undirected bipartite graphs meet the criteria for verification within a reasonable time frame, which is an established fact. Secondly, we have found an efficient algorithm for determining whether a given bipartite graph belongs to a particular spectrum class. Notably, this approach outperforms previous methods, with significant implications, such as directly addressing the feasibility of reducing spectrum verification within a logarithmic-linear time complexity class. Furthermore, it is worth noting that our proof also involves a novel, independent result: the possibility of deciding spectrum membership in a different complexity class, which holds promise for practical applications.

Variants of the electrostatic phase plate (EPPP) have shown promise as an alternative to the glass-type phase plate in enhancing image contrast in transmission electron microscopy. Due to its capability for computer-controlled management, electrostatic rings or pixelated structures serve as PPs offer the flexibility to fine-tune electron probe size and current density. Our study presents a comprehensive analysis of electrostatic PP designs, starting with a complete formulation for calculating probe size and current density, followed by an in-depth examination of the impact of fill-factor and pixel pattern on final probe size and current density. We compared four distinct pixel patterns – random, cross, diamond, and grid – paired with various fill-factor, or split voltage, settings. Our findings suggest that all four pixel patterns yield nearly identical probe sizes at low fill-factor (< 0.5), whereas at high fill-factor (>= 0.5), a considerable increase in probe size is observed with cross, diamond, and grid patterns compared to a randomly pixelated PP. We also found that low split voltages result in higher current densities compared to their geometric mean split voltage, whereas at high split voltages, the relative gain in current is minimal and significantly affected by structural details of the PP. We propose a simple method to estimate the relative current gain based on mean electric field alignment, yet our analysis indicates this approach may lead to inaccuracies due to the complex and delicate phase profile dependence on local field alignment.

We introduce a unified framework to compare physical computation and quantum computation, ultimately determining that quantum computation is a specific type of parallel processing, similar to other known mechanisms. Furthermore, the framework provides a pluralistic perspective on computation, offering a broader understanding of its nature. A crucial element of this evaluation is a generalised model of sequential circuits. We apply this model to elucidate the processes of universal quantum computation and circuit measurement. We also revisit the concept of simulation in computation and the distinction between presence-absence dualism. We discuss the circuit model's capacity to simulate universal quantum computers. However, circuit-based simulation poses several problems. We argue that a more viable approach to modelling computation and its applications is through the process of abstracting universal machines. We also explore the implications of this concept for computational pluralism.

Using a common probabilistic technique for demonstrating asymptotics, we demonstrate that the average number of instances a d-dimensional random walk returns to the origin within n steps is nearly identical to the average number of instances a walk in the higher d+1 dimension does so. We then argue that this shared property can be employed to simpler, more intuitive proofs of the phenomena's asymptotic behavior.

This study explores a model of polymer black hole that exhibits non-classical properties, featuring a wormhole at its core. The model, represented by a general relativistic effect, contains a hexagonal graph that generates the characteristic polymerization parameter. As one approaches the central singularity, the curvature scalar diverges in a finite amount of time, effectively replacing the classical black hole with a wormhole. Analysis of the metric function and curvature scalars indicates that this transition can be interpreted as a graceful exit from the big crunch, resulting from effective quantum backreaction. Further investigation into the curvature invariants and embedded surfaces reveals a smooth transition from black hole characteristics to a wormhole structure, with the curvature of the horizon remaining finite. Counterintuitively, we find that the curvature scalar within the horizon is lower than outside, with the former being quantum in nature. As the curvature of the horizon decreases and reaches zero, the associated entropy also diminishes and becomes zero, thus satisfying the second law of thermodynamics. However, to satisfy all energy conditions, a matter with exotic properties is required in this model.

We investigated the link between the renormalized quasiparticle velocity and
vector boson mass, and discovered that this connection leads to a unique relationship
between the quasiparticle velocity and various physical properties of doped graphene.
These properties include the heat capacity, spin susceptibility, and plasma frequency.
Our computational method allowed us to calculate the renormalization of the boson
mass and velocity up to four-loop precision in the Euler renormalization scheme.
The outcomes of our study revealed that at low temperatures, the heat capacity in
doped graphene can deviate significantly from theoretical predictions. The extent
of this deviation depends on the UV cut-off scale and can even lead to a non-Fermi
liquid phase. The plasmmon frequency in doped graphene also exhibits unusual
behavior, decreasing as the momentum increases and ultimately falling below the
rest mass of the vector boson.

A novel generative model called MaskedSpeech has been developed to synthesize high-quality speech with a level of flexibility comparable to that of TTS systems. By employing a novel masking strategy to hide speech features and utilizing a training approach that combines self-supervision and task-specific guidance, the model is capable of producing speech that is both natural and expressive, while also allowing for the fine-tuning of speech characteristics such as gender and tone. Evaluation shows that MaskedSpeech achieves significant reductions in reconstruction error when compared to other generative models and even surpasses traditional TTS systems in terms of accuracy.

High-dimensional posterior contraction is an important issue in Bayesian variable selection. A new method called Smallest Valid Posterior contraction (SVPost) is proposed to support consistent posterior contraction of the full model. By integrating computational efficiency into SVPost, the approach not only maintains the contraction properties of the original method but also retains its uncertainties. Furthermore, SVPost adapts to sparse model settings while preserving its benefits. A general framework is established for implementing SVPost across various variable selection methods, including Stan, PyMC3, and Glint, which demonstrates the method's efficiency in post-processing existing models.

This paper examines different types of attacks that can compromise Deep Neural Networks, focusing on the limitations and variations of Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks in comparison to adversarial examples. An important distinction between these attack types is that MitM attacks involve altering a model's predictions or inputs, whereas adversarial examples are designed to remain unchanged, thereby limiting their applicability in certain scenarios. The paper tailors a game-theoretic model to deepen the understanding of this issue by analyzing situations where an adversary seeks to maximize their gains while minimizing alterations to inputs, under conditions of constrained attack capabilities. Notably, the study reveals that an attacker employing simple adversarial examples can effectively fool a learning algorithm by utilizing minimal modification to inputs in most cases. The paper further proposes a defensive strategy for attackers, along with a polynomial-time algorithm for implementing it.

Recent research has established a link between climate change denial and online conspiracy theories. However, the underlying reasons for this connection remain unclear. To gain insights, we examined climate change-related content within the conspiracy theory ecosystem by analyzing a large dataset of online conspiracy forums, articles, and channels on prominent conspiracy theory platforms. Our findings suggest that a network of coordinated conspiracy influencers plays a significant role in spreading climate change denial through climate change modules that emphasize a global conspiracy led by specific organizations and individuals to suppress the perceived reality of climate change. Furthermore, our research reveals that climate change denial modules are more prevalent among male conspiracy influencers and that there exists a distinct emphasis on the conspiracy theory that climate change is induced by toxic man-made pollutants, also known as the "Emissions Change Module."

Researchers conducted an in-depth analysis of proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. With a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and a corresponding data set with a low luminosity of 139 inverse femtobarns, studies were focused on possible dark matter production alongside highly energetic isolated particles. These included particles with significant transverse momentum or light hadronic clusters. No deviations from the standard model predictions were detected, and new heavy dark matter candidates interacting through a mediator particle have been ruled out across various models. Outcomes indicate that dark matter candidates with low mass can have a wide range of upper limits on their interaction cross-sections, which span from the weakly interacting massive particle models to the simplified models and the hidden valence quark models.

In a general exangulated category with boundaries, we determine the requirements for Serre duality to hold by providing an equivalent condition. This allows us to broaden a previous theorem. Furthermore, we show that for any exangulated category with boundaries, there is a corresponding exangulated category with Serre duality that has a full subcategory equivalent to the original category, also possessing Serre duality. This relationship can be applied to various categories such as G-exangulated categories, m-exangulated categories, and star-exangulated categories.

Individual educational choices are largely independent, yet their collective outcome often leads to a suboptimal level of human capital development due to individuals failing to account for supply and demand dynamics in the labor market. To address this disparity, we introduce a market-based informational intervention, which informs students about future supply and demand conditions and associated financial benefits. Field-specific information correction levels are determined by current discrepancies and associated economic costs. These costs arise from the difference between actual and socially efficient quantities of field-specific graduates. We evaluate the policy's effectiveness in the fields of study with the highest and lowest average earnings in post-secondary programs across Norway, Denmark, Sweden, and Finland, basing our analysis on historical data from around 1995 to 2015, comparing the dynamic that would have occurred without policy to the observed convergence dynamic under policy implementation. Our results indicate that the policy causes a significant increase in students choosing higher-paying fields of study, with post-secondary fields of study having above-average payoffs seeing reduced convergence between actual and efficient quantities by approximately 16 percent, compared to a 40 percent reduction in fields with above-average payoffs. Notably, the policy's effectiveness varies by country, with above-average payoffs observing a 70 percent reduced convergence, while countries with countries with above-average payoffs observing a 30 percent reduced convergence.

The Belle II experiment, based at the KEK facility in Japan, is an advanced particle physics facility that operates as a super J/$\phi$ factory, providing an abundant supply of $c\bar{c}$ and $b\bar{b}$ antiparticle pairs in both electron-positron collisions and $\phi$ decays. With an anticipated operating luminosity of around $10^{35}$ cm$^{-2}$/s, this experiment will gather a massive total dataset of approximately 20 ab$^{-1}$ over the course of a decade. As a result of this enormous data collection, numerous new research opportunities will be unlocked, enabling the precise reevaluation of previously established results, enhancement of statistical significance for previously discovered rare processes, and further exploration of the flavor anomalies and the search for new physics, particularly in the context of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment and the rare decay $B_s^0\rightarrow\mu^+\mu^-$.

We simulated the accretion of a triple star system via direct N-body 
calculations, accounting for a stellar mass ratio $q = 0.1$ and a triple 
configuration on either a linear or triangular orbit. Our model included a 
global box with a mass capture factor $\log_{10}(f) = -2$, a star formation 
rate $\dot{\Gamma} = 10^{-7} M_{\odot} \text{yr}^{-1}$, and a 
protoplanetary disk around each of the three stars. 

Our findings indicate that in a hierarchical system, the inner binary's 
accretion behavior mirrors that of a single star of equivalent mass, 
whereas any significant accretion by the third, more distant star occurs only 
when the orbital structure shifts due to gas interactions. 

Additionally, our simulations reveal that on a timescale of 
$\sim 10^{7}\text{yr}$, a triple star system with mass ratio $q = 0.1$ is 
unlikely to form a protoplan if all three stars reside within a resolved 
orbit. 

These results imply that hierarchical stellar systems are not an ideal 
setting for the early formation of planets compared to isolated stars. 

These simulations form part of a broader project to assess the potential 
for exoplanet discovery through changes in the position of nearby stars, 
particularly in systems containing young triple stars.

This paper explores inhomogeneous models of the universe with a focus on how a non-uniform distribution of matter influences cosmic structure and evolution. Researchers are revisiting cosmological data, seeking to determine if the Big Bang's assumptions of homogeneity and isotropy are valid. Inhomogeneous geometry was initially proposed to explain the observed acceleration of the universe's expansion, reducing the need for a dark energy component. We examine several key aspects relevant to current data, inhomogeneous models, and their implications for the future of cosmology.

We introduce a novel numerical method for broken pixel images, extending the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model to segment them more efficiently. Our approach differs from existing methods, which typically employ total variation or $L^1$ norms in $L^2$ spaces, by introducing a piecewise constant structure. To accurately represent the image, we utilize a piecewise constant gradient representation with bounded values, utilizing WEnG spaces. This allows us to precisely capture image features and achieve better segmentation results. Our method demonstrates improved segmentation performance over state-of-the-art techniques on various images, including corrupted and BPSM type binary images, and can be easily decomposed and scaled for high-dimensional applications. Furthermore, our method boasts strong theoretical convergence properties and provides a pratical and effective solution for image segmentation.

Ultralight dark matter particles, with masses at or below $10^{-22}$ eV, are often referred to as "dark matter waves." These particles present an unusual opportunity to study quantum mechanics on cosmological scales, as their quantum wavefunction may become distorted by gravitational interactions. This distortion could lead to observable interference patterns, potentially solving long-standing puzzles in dark matter research. This paper explores how wave-like behavior might impact cosmic structure formation and makes predictions for how it could be detected through imaging. Furthermore, the study considers how alternative quantum theories could lead to observable differences in the universe's large-scale structure. Ultimately, this work underscores the importance of cosmic observations in testing quantum mechanics beyond its traditional bounds.

In the field of computing, there's a growing interest in developing power-efficient systems by leveraging on-chip spatial parallelism between neurons and pixels. This approach to neural computing, where pattern recognition and prediction are combined, can learn online without the need for supervision. A novel spike-based recursive algorithm is proposed in this work to enable neural networks with multi-layered architectures to train themselves in real-time. Using a convolutional neural network on a neuromorphic chip, the algorithm achieves superior performance at an extremely low power consumption level of around 100 milliwatts.

A remarkable in-situ observation of the coronal KIP-5 storm revealed the evolution of plasma noise in a complex coronal hole. This evolution was characterized by two distinct phases, characterized respectively by an intense noise storm and a lesser intensity but expansive noise storm. This phenomenon can be explained through the existence of two noise sources, whose intensity, size and noise frequency differ, although their sizes are of comparable magnitude. These two modes, referred to as the "sausage" mode, were also supported by MHD simulations and could be reconciled with the results of Far UV and optical observations of the coronal hole. This "sausage" model offers a promising framework for further studies of plasma dynamics.

We present a novel maneuver to transfer neutral rubidium atoms from a vacuum chamber into a separate optical trap using a highly directed jet, enabling the creation of an extremely compact and integrated optically pumped resonance light scattering magnetometer by means of cross-chamber coupling. The efficiency of this atom transfer method exceeds $90\%$, resulting in a substantial flow of atoms into the detection area and allowing for a considerable reduction in the required detection volume and associated laser power. The presselection of a specific velocity range of $8.5\pm0.5$ cm/s ensures efficient magnetometry with a standard deviation of $3\%$ and guarantees the atoms' sufficient residence time in the detection area for accurate measurement of their spin precession. By combining this technique with OPTICO, a resonant, optically detected magnetometer based on spin-precession imaging, we achieve a precision of $10\%$ in magnetic field measurement, equivalent to $16$ atoms per detection interval, with a resolution of $4$ fT$\sqrt{\text{Hz}^{-1}}$.

The paucity of luminosity in supermassive black holes such as Sgr A* and M87* may be a consequence of luminosity regulation mechanisms, and this study presents the first detailed linear stability analysis of such a potential process - radiation pressure driven thermal disk instability (RP-TDI). Utilizing modern accretion disk hydrodynamics, the research finds that RP-TDI is capable of sustaining thermal balance at all scales, including the supermassive black hole range, and further reveals that the factor of luminosity to Eddington ratio is conserved across varying masses, and that the paucity of luminosity in M87* and Sgr A* can be explained by a single, universally applicable threshold value of the luminosity to Eddington ratio. Moreover, RP-TDI is found to be a plausible mechanism for explaining various multi-messenger observations of compact luminous sources and active galactic nuclei, and the variability timescales of such systems, and the results of this work imply that luminosity in accreting black holes, from the smallest stellar-mass entities to the largest supermassive ones, could all be governed by a unified, pressure-driven disk instability.

We explore the L\"owdin theory with an emphasis on the Lorentz condition in the context of a two-level atom near a perfect reflector, via both a quantum electric field and a quantum radiation stress-energy density. The atom is assumed to emit photons at a single frequency. Applying a non-relativistic, non-quantum mechanical buffer to the atom's motion, we calculate the rate of spontaneous photon emission. To first-order relativistic correction, we derive the rate of photon emission. The result indicates that the atom's initial velocity influences the photon emission rate, leading to a modified, velocity-dependent A-coefficient that could potentially explain the observed 6cm and 21cm hydrogen line cosmological phenomena.

Our analysis of massive star distribution and spatial velocity within the young cluster Westerlund 2 reveals key insights into its formation and evolution. Leveraging high-quality data from multiple sources, including stellar catalogues obtained through optical and infrared spectroscopy, we construct the cluster's colour-magnitude diagram and calculate spatial and phasor efficiencies of massive star ejection. Our findings suggest that Westerlund 2 experienced multiple star-forming episodes and contains at least two distinct stellar populations. Furthermore, our research indicates a lower bound for massive star ejection efficiency of $0.15\pm0.05$, consistent with findings from other young massive clusters, but star formation in Westerlund 2 may have been regulated by its massive stars due to their feedback mechanisms.

The first nontrivial example of a minimax principle has been a significant source of numerous existence results for various problems in both nonlinear analysis and topology. The purpose of this paper is to explore a specific class of variational problems that have a guaranteed solution under specific conditions, aligning with the principles established by Ambrosetti and Rabinowitz in their seminal work from 1973. The specific problem considered here involves a proper lower semicontinuous function defined over a subset of a separable Hilbert space with countable sublevels. Our approach utilizes countable subcovers as a key tool in demonstrating the existence of a solution for variational problems. This study extends previous works, such as those of Aubin from 1968 and Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis in 1996, and also covers variational problems on spaces that may not be compact. Our findings indicate that countable sublevels play a crucial role in ensuring the existence of a minimum for any lower semicontinuous function defined over separable Hilbert spaces.

This research presents a novel framework that integrates a handwritten text recognizer with Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN). The framework automates the enhancement of degraded document images and the recognition of handwritten text. It is based on the observation that a text recognizer can provide textual information to build a highly relevant prior knowledge model of a specific recognizer. The proposed framework alternates between the text recognizer and a generative model in a cooperative manner to enhance each other's performance. It includes a supplementary recognition module that optimizes the input for the main text recognizer. The framework is demonstrated on both synthetic and real-world handwritten documents, and its effects on recognition accuracy are analyzed.

Text extraction from id cards presents complex challenges, largely due to id cards' varied design. To tackle these challenges, an innovative approach combining the precise image processing of OpenCV and the advanced pattern recognition of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has been developed to efficiently extract text from various id cards. While existing image processing methods focus on general purposes, this approach is tailored to id cards and has demonstrated remarkable results, achieving a 97% success rate in extracting text from Chinese id cards and a 95% success rate in extracting text from driver's licenses.

In complex scenarios where multiple reflective surfaces interact with both transmitter and receiver, along with a multitude of scatterers, channel estimation becomes a challenging task. This problem is further compounded by high mobility of the user equipment. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative channel estimation technique that leverages long short term memory networks to exploit the temporal correlations within the channel. Our simulation results demonstrate that this approach yields substantial improvements in channel estimation accuracy, particularly in scenarios characterized by high mobility.

We leverage astronomical image super-resolution to improve image quality in a low-resolution setting, combining a pre-trained generator with an innovative discriminator. The primary contribution of this research lies in developing a more effective discriminator to augment the generator. Initially, our method involves training a discriminator using high-resolution images as targets. Subsequently, this discriminator is reused for low-resolution images, but with the goals expanded to include image fidelity and image realism. By integrating features from original, log, and high-frequency images, our proposed discriminator significantly outperforms existing AP-GP and SRGAN methods.

A novel optimization framework is proposed, integrating feedforward neural networks with a mathematical representation of physical conservation laws to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). In this framework, the dataset of solution points is progressively adjusted during the training process to minimize the predicted error in the network's output. An important feature of this algorithm is its ability to avoid overfitting by continuously incorporating new stochastic noise into the dataset. While traditionally, the conservation laws are incorporated into the loss function as in the Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) approach, this framework treats them as a means to refine the training dataset itself.

In 2019, the ECFA Early Career Researcher (ECR) panel was established with four members and officially started its operations in 2020. During the first two years of its operation, the panel handled ECR applications separately from the general community applications. Two hundred and twenty-seven applications were received and extensively evaluated through a combination of recommendations, in-person discussions at ECFA general assemblies, and virtual meetings. The applications were categorized into three areas: individual ECR applications, group applications from research groups led by early-career researchers, and department-level applications. The results have influenced ECNA policy decisions regarding appointments and promotions to the Nine-member Appointments and Promotions panel.

This study presents an innovative method to control line waves within the optical regime by employing a single type of line resonator integrated into a graphene patch with an unconventional design. By introducing a second graphenae patch for multi-wavelength operation, the proposed structure showcases the potential for dynamic control of line waves through the electrical biasing of both graphene layers. Furthermore, the research investigates the impact of line resonator orientation on coupling efficiency with line waves and offers comprehensive analysis of the proposed structure's performance, including a discussion on its potential applications in line wave multiplexing based on frequency and orientation.

This study presents a novel approach to multi-human multi-robot interaction (HMI-HRRI) through Federated Learning (FL). Employing FL for this application brings several benefits, including secure multi-agent collaboration, consistent robot behavior across different robots, and the maintenance of individual user anonymity. In our framework, a primary server uses FL to gather knowledge from multiple humans, who train their unique models using shared data without ever exchanging it, thereby contributing to a universal knowledge base also accessible to service robots. The study presents a FL-based system for real-world social recognition tasks and demonstrates its effectiveness through both simulation and experimental results. Additionally, we introduce a novel evaluation protocol capable of measuring a model's transferability of social knowledge in a real-world setting.

A novel method of bias-reduced estimation is proposed, utilizing an arbitrary initial density estimate that doesn't require prior smoothness assumptions. The bias correction process involves solely first-order derivatives, resulting in a enhanced estimator with improved smoothness properties. Specific examples of this bias-reduced estimator are demonstrated for both the normal distribution and a bivariate normal distribution.

A common approach in link prediction involves using a subgraph derived from a knowledge graph, which includes entities and their connections. Since this method relies on the structure of the knowledge graph, it indirectly depends on data obtained through relation extraction. This study provides an explicit framework for incorporating the information gained from relation learning into link prediction. It involves creating an explicit semantic model of the knowledge entities by translating the relationship between their representations into a specific logical format. After that, a logical knowledge graph is constructed based on this representation system. Finally, a novel approach to link prediction is developed, utilizing the full understanding of the knowledge graph, which includes both its structure and content. This new approach outperforms standard techniques using a range of large knowledge graph datasets, and showcases the importance of modeling both semantic and syntactic language aspects in the knowledge graph.

In the context of three-flavor massive IIB string theory and its associated dual $SU(3) \times SU(3)$ conformal field theory, the DE model's Debye mass is found to be unaffected by the adjoint scalar VEV and instead mirrors the type IIA result under thermal conditions without a baryonic potential. When a baryonic potential is introduced, however, the Debye mass in type IIB theory exhibits a multiplicity of three times that of type IIA. Furthermore, in type IIB theory, the DE model's Debye and undoped Turyan-Mcflow Debye masses are discovered to be indistinguishable. When a trilinear potential is present in the superpotential of type IIB theory, the theory develops a linear relationship in space for the temperature-dependent undoped Debye mass. For the massless case in type IIB theory with a baryonic potential, a model based on an $SU(2) N=1$ vector model is introduced in three-dimensional space. By applying a mean-field theory to the theory, a method is found to calculate the baryonic potential's impact on the undoped Debye mass, which is found to equate the model's undoped and turysan-mcflow Debye masses. An approach is found to determine the baryonic potential's impact on the undoped Debye mass, which relates to the type IIA result with a coefficient of 8/

A detailed study of the magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 was conducted using neutron diffraction to examine the magnetic configurations of both the rare earth and transition metal ions in these compounds. Both Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 display a crystalline structure where the rare earth and transition metal ions form layers aligned perpendicularly. Research indicates that within each of these materials, the transition metal ions are organized into a striped pattern, with rare earth magnetic configurations that exhibit a combination of antiferromagnetism and ferromagnetism. Notably, in Tb3RuO7, a previously unobserved magnetic state with all ions aligned was discovered using neutron diffraction, which can be stabilized through an external magnetic field. This state represents a significant departure from the material's ground state, which is stabilized through a series of magnetic phase transitions. Additionally, it was found that when Tbridging Ru ions are surrounded by rare earth magnetic configurations that are antiferromagnetic, they prefer to adopt a spin state with an arrangement that is antiferromagnetic with respect to the primary magnetic ions. Conversely, in ferromagnetic compounds, these transition metal ions display a variety of complex magnetic configurations, which may be stabilized through a variety of local exchange interactions.

A novel local-functional model is proposed, transforming fixed-length signal segments into latent codes via a neural network and mapping them to a target space using another network. The study demonstrates local-functional outperforms traditional end-to-end end-to-end models for real-world audio tasks, achieving better generation quality and signal reconstruction accuracy. Notably, local-functional exhibits enhanced generalization capabilities for lower dimensional signals, achieved through gradient-based optimization of a latent code regularization term during training. Furthermore, the analysis reveals local-functional offers the theoretical potential for better sample generation in real-world applications.

This paper presents a semi-generative model that utilizes sub-causal variables, enabling it to represent the intricate dependencies of a target variable via both its causal factors and their respective outcomes. In contrast to conventional variational autoencoders, which can only convey condensed representations of past data to a generation model, our approach allows specific representations to convey detailed information about both causal factors and their respective effects. Consequently, this model offers a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying characteristics of a target variable, potentially facilitating variable independence in the generated output. We tested this approach on several real-world datasets and found it successfully reduced dependency between the predicted outcome variable and the other measured variables in the proposed cause-and-effect model. Ultimately, we argue that our model offers a more interpretable representation of complex causal systems.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning technologies have sparked significant interest in understanding the underlying geometric properties of these systems. The ability to elucidate the geometric behavior of deep learning algorithms and architectures can provide valuable insights, guiding researchers in developing innovative algorithms and structures within the field. Geometry, an ancient discipline, offers a robust framework for mathematical reasoning that is particularly suitable for describing complex systems with large datasets. Geometry's capacity to describe intricate systems through mathematical reasoning makes it a potent tool for guiding deep learning research towards novel discoveries within the manifold learning space.

A computational investigation was conducted to analyze the behavior of lattice 
smallest reduction sets (MRSR) in cubic fields. We define and examine 
MRSR for cubic fields. A computer examination of all relevant sets in cubic fields 
defining totally real extensions revealed patterns based on the field's minimal 
discriminant. These patterns showed that changing a specific irrational number 
in the field's defining polynomial can significantly affect MRSR length. 
Furthermore, our study also explored the relationship between the minimum 
MRSR length and specific lattice reduction algorithms. A hypothesis was formulated 
to limit the possible lengths of MRSR sets.

Relevance propagation has established itself as a popular approach for interpreting the behavior of deep neural networks. Nevertheless, applying this technique to pre-trained models poses significant challenges, primarily due to intricate interactions between weights and gradients that undermine conventional activation backpropagation. In our approach, we tackle this issue by developing a learning scheme for generalized relevance propagation that can be seamlessly integrated with end-to-end learning. This enables us to uncover novel, previously unappreciated properties of ReLU networks, including a strong correlation between gradient flow and reversible information propagation. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed method excels in visual and textual applications, yielding insightful insights into the capacity of neural networks to capture complex concepts and interdependencies.

We introduce r-associated Stirling numbers of the second kind, a modification of the traditional Stirling numbers, which categorize partitions of sets into r-sized subsets. Additionally, we derive key properties and relationships of these numbers, specifically focusing on their recurrence formula and connection to the standard Stirling numbers.

The concept of irreducible domains and boundary interfaces is applied to describe local distortions and structural phase transitions in materials with a layered structure,
where non-linear effects are represented by dislocation densities.
This formalism is used to classify irreducible domains based on breaking of symmetries in 2H transition metal dichalcogenides.
In materials such as MoS$_2$, the size and nature of irreducible domains are linked to the formation of interfaces that break trigonal polar symmetry,
allowing for the creation of electric dipole moments at these boundaries.
By this formalism, it is shown that disclinations can generate localized charges,
while dislocations generally do not due to the absence of long-range strain gradient order parameters.
This approach identifies a strain-gradient electric field that can trap rotationally charged defects, providing guidance for engineering matter-l light interactions in these materials.

The concept of noncommutative geometry offers insights into how the Gabor wavelet can establish a maximal level of possible momentum resolution on a manifold, revealing a fundamental connection between momentum and the curvature of space. This relationship indicates that as the curvature of a manifold increases, so does its inherent noncommutativity. The analysis builds upon earlier research where the author demonstrated the capability of generating tight frames from group representations and relates it to the zero-curvature property shared by the de-Broglie wave and a plane wave. Consequently, quantum mechanics can be interpreted as a manifestation of the spatial properties of matter waves. The author also explores how the absolute square of global sections on a Riemannian manifold contributes to the local metric, offering an interpretation of randomness as a manifestation of local curvature. The discussion concludes by relating these findings to stochastic thermodynamics.

We introduce a novel method to train models using samples from a complex distribution. This model employs complex-valued affine coupling layers, enabling it to work with complex inputs without converting them to real values. Our research shows that the model's probability distribution matches that of real inputs when its parameters are optimized. This research also highlights the benefits of complex affine layers in Monte Carlo simulations, as they generate more efficient samples with lower variance for a given number of passes. Our findings indicate that the models trained with complex affine layers converge faster and perform better in the rare event estimation of neural networks.

A model exploring how U(1)_F flavor symmetry is broken in the context of a left-right symmetric model incorporates bi-doublet scalar fields transforming under both SU(2)_L and SU(2)_R.  The model leverages an approximate U(1)_F symmetry, with the top-bottom mass difference attributed to symmetry breaking via the <Tf_R> / <Tf_L> ratio.  Additional mechanisms utilizing higher dimensional operators explain the left-right symmetry breaking at a scale of approximately 1 TeV and contribute to radiative quadratically sensitive corrections in the potential.  By introducing a Goldstone boson into the meson sector, this study investigates the origin of a small epsilon (0.01) in meson mass.  In a dark matter scenario, a light fermion, compatible with SU(2)_L x U(1)_Y, acts as a candidate, acquiring mass through a scalar field's spontaneous symmetry breaking.  Calculations of the self-interaction cross-section and dark matter-nucleon scattering probabilities are conducted within this framework.

Vulnerability vulnerability exploitation prevention platforms (VPPMs) are a cutting-edge security technology that proactively monitors and prevents malicious activity in virtual machine environments. With the increasing adoption of cloud computing and virtualization, the security provided by VPPMs has become a crucial aspect of maintaining the safety of virtual machine deployments. Although commercial VPPMs are based on machine learning, the underlying algorithms are often shrouded in mystery, making it difficult to assess their effectiveness and reliability. This research introduces a novel testing framework designed to evaluate the vulnerability prevention capabilities of commercial VPPMs. Our approach involves an open-source implementation of popular VPPMs on real-world hardware, allowing for flexible and customizable testing solutions. Using this framework, we assessed the prevention capabilities of two leading commercial VPPMs, revealing impressive attack mitigation rates but also raising concerns about potential abuse and performance impacts. Our findings offer valuable insights for VPPM developers to enhance their products, filling a critical gap in the evaluation of commercial VPPMs.

The success of pre-trained language models in individual languages has prompted researchers to investigate their potential as a unified resource for all languages. Building on recent findings in multilingual NLP, we analyzed the adaptability of pre-trained multilingual models to individual languages using a common benchmark. This comprehensive study evaluated 22 pre-trained models across 59 low-resource languages and revealed three key influences: linguistic lineage, the model's training data, and the size of the training corpus. Notably, our extensive experiment demonstrated that pre-trained language models significantly outperform pre-trained language families in term of adaptability and performance.

Investigating the role of rotation in preventing complete gravitational collapse is a key objective of this research. By employing a simplified 1D model, we are able to analyze the point of onset for a rotationally supported star that undergoes collapse. As a star in a rotating core collapses via accretion, its angular velocity increases due to conservation of angular momentum, which is comparable to the effect of mass growth. According to our research, a core that forms a binary star has a higher mass ratio and lower binary mass when the kinetic energy of rotation is higher relative to the gravitational energy. Conversely, stars that undergo collapse as single stars are more likely to form in cores with lower masses and less rapid rotation. By comparing our model with observational data on mass ratios and masses of nearby stars, we are able to identify several key aspects that align with the effects of rotation. Notably, a significant portion of the observed stars exhibit characteristics such as a mass ratio of nearly one, and the distribution of masses in both binary and single star systems is consistent with a peak at lower masses and a decline at higher masses.

Kernel-based dimensionality reduction techniques like k-d arbritary rank (m-ar-K) offer superior performance due to their resilience to outliers and flexibility in modeling non-convex manifolds. However, existing implementations suffer from high time and space complexities, respectively. In this research, a novel space and time efficient algorithm is devised, leveraging an arborescent tree-based approach reminiscent of the condensed gradient boosting method. By moving away from arborescent trees, the new algorithm significantly reduces space requirements, outperforming alternatives such as kernel principal component analysis in multiple benchmark datasets available at https://github.com/teoychong/chost.

This research investigates computational tasks solvable with assistance from a quantum computer, random oracle, classical interaction, and limited auxiliary power, denoted as EPC. It is noted that a similar model, P^O, has proven useful in qubit quantum query model studies. As P^O equals CPT with an added constraint of limited auxiliary power, a potential super-polynomial EPC lower bound could offer significant insight into the non-equivalence of CPT and PTIME. Conversely, an upper bound for EPC of BPTIME(2^poly) would imply that CPT is contained within this class. To support this, the research proves that P^O is contained in EPC when both models are limited to limited auxiliary power. Furthermore, the research shows that tasks achievable in the quantum computer, interaction, and limited auxiliary power model are also achievable in the circuit model, implying that EPC, without the need for additional power, equals CPT, which in turn contains P^O, both results holding for limited auxiliary power.

A finitely generated ideal in a commutative ring with unity can be expressed as the intersection of a small number of prime ideals, defining an element of the ring. A ring with this property is known as $\tau$-elementary. In a $\tau$-elementary ring, we investigate the local properties of the ring by examining its maximal ideals and how they influence the ring's structure. Specifically, we look at the localizations at non-primal ideals and how they affect the ring's properties. In this process, we find that certain prime ideals in the ring become principal ideals in the localizations. Furthermore, we establish a connection between a ring being $\tau$-elementary and a specific condition involving the ring's unit ideal and its prime ideals, similar to a well-known condition for principal ideal domains. These $\tau$-elementary rings have important applications in various areas of mathematics, including commutative algebra, algebraic geometry, and number theory. In this paper, we show that a commutative catenary domain with a finite number of prime ideals in any chain is $\tau$-elementary if and only if it has dimension one. Additionally, we prove that a Noetherian domain with a finite number of prime ideals in any chain is $\tau$-elementary regardless of its dimension.

Social media platforms like Twitter provide social and political groups with a valuable opportunity to comprehend each other's perspectives. However, the vast amount of social media data often goes unutilised due to its under-explored nature. This research aims to address this gap by developing a comprehensive Twitter data set and an advanced narrative-based sentiment analysis approach. The proposed method recognises social media posts as an extension of their authors' stories, which can be analyzed along with their emotional sentiment. This involves extracting key attributes from tweets, such as notable mentions of individuals or organisations, and combining such embedded narratives with their respective emotional sentiments to calculate the overall sentiment sentiment. This approach is referred to as narrative sentiment analysis. Our research employs the political discourse surrounding Brexit on Twitter to evaluate the proposed method's effectiveness. By grouping Brexiteers based on their shared narratives and sentiment, four distinct discourse segments were identified, namely: Moderate Pro-EU, Hardline Pro-EU, Moderate Pro-Leg, and Hardline Pro-Leg. These categories provide a clearer picture of the emotional and sentiment-driven political landscape.

This work presents a novel deep learning-based system for automatically detecting and localising events in video streams with spatial precision. Unlike prior approaches, which assume a fixed spatial resolution, our strategy accommodates events occurring across different spatial scales. By employing a single binary classification network with a dynamically adjustable spatial resolution through a novel novel dynamic pyramidal feature fusion approach, our system effectively handles variability in spatial dimensions. Furthermore, our approach leverages context-specific features that evolve in tandem with the resolution. The effectiveness of our method has been substantiated through comprehensive experiments on widely recognised datasets, including SSFlow, P2P-Tebis, and sign language datasets sign language datasets sign language datasets, showcasing superior performance and robustness to spatial resolution changes.

The relationship between the distribution of CMB lensing potential and the spatial arrangement of galaxies is influenced by the inflationary model's properties, which also determine the relationship between matter density and cluster counts across different time periods. This connection can be exploited within a Bayesian framework using cluster redshift distributions and weak lensing data to estimate the relationship between lensing potential and cluster count probabilities. The required data can be obtained from current and upcoming surveys of the CMB, galaxies, and cluster redshifts. By incorporating lensing data on this scale, it is possible to isolate cosmological parameters from redshift-space distortion parameters and potentially gain insight into the relationship between lensing potential and cluster counts. This information is valuable for distinguishing between the $\Lambda$CDM model and alternative inflationary models. By analyzing the lensing potential's effect on the relationship between lensing potential and cluster counts, it is possible to determine lensing-based cosmological parameters independently, using only lensing data to determine some of these parameters. These parameters can then serve as a robust set of lensing-based measurements to cross-verify with other types of measurements.

The LPMR framework integrates theoretical concepts from adversarial robustness and group representation learning to develop a model that can withstand and detect perturbations. By forming a robust feature space using groups of samples perturbed during training, our method enhances model resilience against worst-case disturbances through feature alignment. Extensive experiments on image classification tasks demonstrate that our approach surpasses current robust learning methods in terms of accuracy under both natural and artificial attacks, along with improved generalization capabilities.

The sudden appearance of novel rumors on online platforms can cause significant disruption to the virtual environment and cause widespread confusion to online users. Existing approaches to neutralizing rumors generally model the diffusion of fake news and malicious comments as a precursor and peak phase, followed by an attenuation period, using a combination of phase-based and feature-based strategies. The main objective of phase-based methods is to delay the attenuation of novel rumors and reduce their final impact. The effectiveness of these methods heavily relies on the accuracy of the phasing model, which is often based on simple linear assumptions. The contributions of online users during the peak phase can have a lasting effect even after the novel rumor enters the attenuation phase. This work aims to deepen the understanding of how features and location information influence the novel rumor neutralization process. The work offers three key advancements: (a) a new approach to delay the attenuation process of novel rumors, taking into account the characteristics of features and the attack on online locations; (b) a modified phase-based method that considers feature and location information during the novel rumor neutralization process; and (c) an explanation of how feature and location information affects the peak and attenuation coefficients of novel rumors. The experiments demonstrate that the proposed novel approach effectively minimizes the harm caused by novel rumors.

This study introduces a novel approach for hyper-spectral pixel classification that leverages dimensionality reduction techniques. By employing unsupervised re-training of these models using only labeled images, it has been found that certain methods possess superior signal reconstruction capabilities, which in turn enhances classification accuracy when the image is re-reconstructed. A new, efficient feature fusion method has also Introduced to enhance classification performance while significantly reducing the required training time. Moreover, the study reveals that these dimensionality reduction methods can effectively function even when re-training involves minimal reconstruction. An efficient training approach further demonstrates notable improvements in classification accuracy when dealing with images that have been reintroduced. Consequently, the study substantially accelerates the time needed to train and analyze hyper-spectral images.

Deep neural networks excel in various fields such as speech and vision, but their high computational requirements can be a significant drawback, particularly when deployed on devices with limited processing capabilities. To overcome this issue, a range of compression techniques have been developed that utilize model pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation as well as novel approaches like structured and unstructured decomposition. Despite their effectiveness, these methods often necessitate a substantial amount of training time and memory. In this research, an compression method is proposed for deep neural networks involving just one concise update, thereby reducing the computational cost and making the process more efficient. The efficiency of the proposed technique is demonstrated on several compression tasks including model quantization, distillation, and a general compression method for deep neural networks.

ProProStructure, previously known as ProStructure, is designed to generate accurate protein structures based on a given sequence of amino acids. Despite its earlier version achieving remarkable results under specific constraints, the ProProStructure system has been limited to producing precise protein structures within 100 amino acids. In this study, an advanced method called ProCoil-2 was introduced to accurately predict coil regions in proteins. By leveraging the breakthroughs of ProCoil-2 and employing a more efficient energy prediction system, the ProProStructure group succeeded in producing high-quality protein structures beyond the 2000 amino acids mark. In this study, an in-depth analysis of the ProProStructure system's design and its utilization of multiple energies and samplers is presented. By integrating these components, the ProProStructure system has surpassed the 2000 amino acid barrier and achieved precise predictions for numerous large proteins, including precise predictions for 2L, 2R amino acid coordinates in a particular 2111 amino acid protein.

This study introduces a novel method to optimize loss functions for better performance on specific tasks, particularly for non-traditional loss functions like KL Divergence that have historically been outperformed by more conventional alternatives. We propose a new framework to develop a task-specific loss function from any given, potentially understudied, base loss. The framework's simplicity and broad applicability allow it to be easily extended to a wide range of loss functions and domains, including vision and language applications. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework across diverse scenarios, revealing significant improvements over baseline benchmarks and baseline loss functions. Furthermore, our research sheds light on the connection between different optimization objectives, offering new insights into the world of machine learning loss functions. The accompanying source code is available at https://github.com/alexbewley/adaptive-loss.

Using the fully interacting Hamiltonian of the parquet equations in a way that preserves their nonperturbative nature, we apply a dynamic approach that leads to an alternative expression for the parquet amplitude. This new amplitude, whose strength is determined by the correlation energy, satisfies neither conservation nor crossing symmetry, unlike the conventional parquet amplitude. Although conservation and crossing symmetry are not inherently present in the standard parquet amplitude, we find that using the core correlation energy as a correction in the scattering matrix restores these properties at the leading order of correlation effects. Additionally, we demonstrate that the variations in the potential due to changes in electron count maintain momentum conservation, thus allowing the restored amplitude to approximate crossing symmetry. As a result, we develop a correction term to enhance the parquet approach.

The two-dimensional material TiSe2 exhibits a rich phenomenon of superconductivity and charge-density-wave effects. Studies suggest that in bulk TiSe2, exciton condensation plays a significant role in the charge-density-wave state, and this concept has been further supported by a theoretical model. This material's properties make it an ideal example for examining the quantum Hall effect in the presence of a strong electron-electron interaction. We have investigated the linear response of monolayer TiSe2 to an external electric field using a theoretical electron model combined with density-functional theory, and our results show that the material displays a distinct peak in the Hall conductivity at a specific Landau level filling of -6 in experimental conditions. This finding signifies a potential for experimental verification of the exciton condensation mechanism through a precise search for the Landau levels in monolayer TiSe2.

In text-based risk reporting systems, dispatchers play a crucial role in gathering essential information from reporters to accurately categorize and process various events. Although dispatchers receive comprehensive training for this purpose, there is currently a lack of research examining their actual practices in different event categories. Through a qualitative study with 12 experienced firefighters in Montreal, Canada, our results reveal that dispatchers tend to collect more information from users in non-fire and lower-severity fire events, compared to life-threatening fire emergencies. These results indicate a potential issue, given that accurate information and timely responses are essential for responding to these events effectively. In contrast, dispatchers commonly prioritize confirming the fire's presence and gathering essential information for processing non-fire and lower-severity fire emergencies. To address this, we discuss system design implications that can support dispatchers in gathering necessary information and effectively inform relevant responses.

We calculated the contributions of line nodes in a multi-dimensional topologically complex node-like structure to key superconducting properties, including heat capacity, magnetic susceptibility, and upper critical field. These calculations were based on the line node's geometric characteristics, such as its distance from the Fermi surface and angular dependence of the gap function. Our findings can serve as an overview of the line node's impact on superconducting behavior and guide experimental identification of specific line node types in superconductors with known node structure. Additionally, we developed a numerical method to determine Ginzburg-Landau critical mass by accounting for the line node geometry, which we applied to the node structure in UTe2. This approach allows the incorporation of anisotropic effective mass and other geometric parameters, making it suitable for a wide range of line node types. Moreover, we showed that the orientation of line nodes relative to the magnetic field has little effect on the magnetic susceptibility or upper critical field at low temperatures, but it significantly influences the Ginzburg-Landau critical mass, especially in superconductors with a multi-band Fermi surface.

A novel, semi-supervised active learning algorithm based on minimax entropy is proposed, aiming to enhance the efficiency of learning models using a limited number of unlabeled samples. To address uncertainty and diversity in sample selection for training, a generalized entropy formulation is adopted and specialized for active learning. The resulting algorithm selects multiple unlabeled samples per iteration, based on a generalized entropy principle that accounts for the interrelationships and class representations of selected samples. This approach generalizes existing uncertainty and diversity-based selection methods and offers improved adaptability to class representations compared to traditional approaches. Furthermore, the algorithm's performance in multi-class settings is rigorously evaluated through theoretical analysis and experimental verification.

In the digital age, vast repositories of music enable research into the evolution of popular song timbre characteristics. Our analysis of nearly 500,000 songs from six major genres reveals that similarity of timbre among songs is not solely driven by individual artist styles but also shows distinct patterns within each genre. The genre-based trends in similarity suggest that distinct sonic identities are formed and persist across decades. Employing a deep neural network style transfer technique, we examine if these longitudinal sonic patterns can be considered formulative of each genre's identity. Evaluating the reconstructed discographies, our findings indicate that a non-random distribution of artistic styles is present, supporting the existence of a formulative sonic identity for each genre. Furthermore, analysis of individual artists' catalogs reveals that many establish a consistent style throughout their careers, validating the concept of a formulative sonic identity. Our study's insights into the longitudinal evolution of music style can inform automatic style attribution and uncover hidden connections between artists. Code for our research is publicly available.

This investigation examines a class of stochastic processes influenced by reinforcement under certain weak assumptions, focusing particularly on their long-term temporal properties. Under these circumstances, we establish the counterintuitive finding that the block structure formed by early stages of a process persists through to the end, despite the inherent randomness and reinforcement influences, thereby providing a novel result in understanding this phenomenon. Our analysis yields several significant consequences, including a precise characterization of the process change-point, proof of the block's infinite duration, and characterization of the block's measure-dependent properties. In addition to the block process analysis, we develop an accelerated version, revealing additional properties and links to existing processes such as Markov processes with a known spectral gap. We provide a detailed explanation of the block process, its properties, and the implications of our research.

The concept of containment, conceptually clear and straightforward, has garnered attention in the context of contemporary meaning-based approaches.  Despite the broader interest in such frameworks, research has been particularly concentrated within the context of natural language processing.  Building upon the work of Dutilh Novaes and Contreras, this paper explores the concept of containment and its inherent 'conceptual inference' or 'constitutive inference' within the context of proof-theoretic semantics.  It reveals that containment, the converse principle, and constitutive inference are mutually interconnected, leading to potential challenges in the context of the framework when these principles are applied.  Consequently, the paper offers the innovative solution of introducing asymmetric containment, aiming to mitigate any potential problems of circularity within the context of the framework.

Reward learning from human feedback often incurs high costs due to the need for numerous human judgments. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to efficiently utilize human annotations by leveraging comparisons rather than rankings. By applying the DiffPolicy method and querying human annotators about the performance of action pairs, we develop a more interaction-efficient framework. Through the application of the Elo rating system, we effectively maintain a representation of reward relevant actions, ultimately leading to a significant reduction in required annotations without compromising quality.

The Smyth powerspace construction, a standard way to create a lattice of closed sets from a core-compact space, does not necessarily maintain core-compactness. It is shown that under specific conditions, such as when the original space has a covering of its binary closed sets by its open parts, the power space will maintain core-compactness.

Building on earlier research by Chen, Mastropietro and the author, where two interlinked Ginzburg-Landab vortex loops in three-dimensional space were studied, this paper extends the investigation to a specific scenario: the configuration of these looped vortices has a topology equivalent to a three-dimensional surface, and the vortices' configuration space can be reduced to a two-dimensional enclosed area, denoted as $\mathcal{A}$. After presenting a parameterization for this space, a new parameter is introduced to distill the v entangled state of the vortices, subsequently deriving an expansion for the free energy based on this parameter, with the initial term derived analytically and higher-order terms estimated numerically.

Double machine learning approaches can mitigate biases from algorithmic decision-making by relying on specially constructed estimators that eliminate interactions between variables and using regularized machine learning algorithms to achieve this. Our research begins by analyzing the bias remaining after double machine learning adjustments and finds that omitting regularization in machine learning components results in suboptimal performance even when test data is utilized. Overting the typical practice of prioritizing regularized estimators like Lasso, we suggest that allocating part of the double machine learning adjustment to regularized machine learning components can enhance overall performance. These findings are supported by simulations, empirical evaluations, and theoretical proof showing that regularizing the AIPW estimator reduces its bias in a manner proportional to its variance. Our experiments further validate the proposed estimation method on two 'real-world' datasets, along with an analysis of its impact on decisions in both micro and macro realms.

The inclusion of a massive tau particle presents significant challenges in theoretical and experimental studies yet its short lifetime allows for direct observation without the need to produce decay products only. Researchers in theoretical particle physics explore tau properties through various means, including lattice QCD simulations and calculations based on the Standard Model. This review covers recent lattice calculations of the tau particle's mass and the axial anomaly constant, as well as the model-dependent parameter $f_V$ in the finite energy sum rules analysis of the $R_{\tau}$ quantity. These studies are contextualized by introducing the basic measurement of the $R_{\tau}$ quantity and its associated theoretical uncertainties.

In a rotation-dominated setting, experiments are conducted using a rotating annulus setup with a pressure sensor to study surface manifestations of baroclinic waves. When the outer wall induces a thermal gradient, wave patterns emerge on the surface that echo their structural origins in the cross-sectional plane. Through wavelet coherence analysis, these surface waves are characterized in terms of wavelength, wave period, and phase relationship with thermal driving forces. For wavelengths exceeding 10 experimental radii and periods exceeding 5 revolutions per radius, surface waves manifest as coherent waves. As the annulus rotates faster or experiences less friction, their wave properties evolve in a manner consistent with 3D wave dynamics, whereas changes in thermal driving forces do not affect their surface manifestation. Furthermore, we employ a theoretical model based on quasi-geostrophic theory, along with a wavelet-based approach to analyze the vertical structure and properties of these waves.

This research proposes a prior framework for quickly prepping Bayesian models that predict rare, extreme events, such as 100-year floods or storms, given observed data, like peak water levels or wind speeds, on a per-location basis. The model comprises two key components: the primary part uses a contemporary Bayesian approach that ties events' magnitudes to their rarity, via a discrete time process in the power domain, whereas the modifying element utilizes predictive inference based on regional data and the selection of a parameter, 'm', influencing estimation accuracy, thereby lending itself to subjective interpretation as precision or smoothness. The paper investigates how regional data enhances estimates of rarer events under various values of 'm', employing simulation methods with real-world data analyses from datasets related to floods and coastal storms. Furthermore, methods for predicting rarer events using regional data are compared, leveraging techniques like leave-one-out cross-validation with model selection.

In robust reinforcement learning, we examine an stochastic bandit multi-armed bandit setting where potential actions produce various outcomes across multiple rewards, with only one reward being revealed after selecting a action. Unlike previous studies, both the extent of the corruption (denoted as $\epsilon$) and the number of arms (actions) are assumed to be unknown. Although knowing the corruption extent enables efficient algorithms for a fixed number of actions, a constant factor loss in regret is inevitable when the corruption extent is unknown. Conversely, regret that is independent of the corruption level is achievable if it is known, but becomes impractically expensive if it is not known, resulting in virtually no action space alternatives. Lastly, we present and evaluate several practical desensitivity methods based on the AdaBoost regrettability framework in numerical experiments.

This study investigates the impulsive heat equation with varying sized control zones, demonstrating that as the number of impulse controls (located at fixed points) increases, a stronger form of impulse approximate controllability can be achieved, thereby implying uniform impulse approximate controllability for the entire class of systems with the following considerations: the number of impulses, the number of control zones, and the system's initial energy level. The required control is estimated through an explicitly expressed functional whose related cost is analyzed using mathematical techniques such as the Titchmarsh convolution theorem and the CauchySchwarz inequality.

The current methods for out-of-distribution detection display significant difficulties on a range of challenge data types, exhibiting an almost indiscriminate ability to identify both in- and out-of-distribution inputs. Despite this issue, the role of data augmentation in enhancing Out-of-Distribution (OOD) identification has not been thoroughly investigated. In this research, we fill this knowledge gap by examining how various data augmentation techniques and OOOD methods perform on the typical benchmark, CAMELs.
