In particular, quality labels refined using edit comments result in assessment models that exhibit higher consistency and better general performance.

Recent research has highlighted significant security concerns with conventional knowledge distillation. To address this, dB3 (decision-based black-box knowledge distillation) offers an innovative approach by leveraging the target model's output decisions rather than its responses. While dB3's potential is promising, specific implementation strategies remain underexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose three dB3 techniques, focusing on (1) addressing data sparsity through support storage, (1b) refining data quality via quality-based storage, and (2) enhancing teacher models via decision-based retrofitting. Experimental results show that our methods surpass a simple baseline and, in some cases, rival the performance of conventional white-label models. Moreover, an additional finding reveals that dB3 provides enhanced robustness against model poisons, underscoring its potential as a significant advancement in this area. All the models referenced in this study, including the distiller and a stringcategorizer classifier, are available at https://github.com/joewright42/DB3.

The relative branching fractions between D*(bar)barb(->)K+pi- and D**-*(s) (->)K+pi- are measured at an average probability of 1.15 with the uncertainty at 16%, based on an sample of 0.76 million D**-*(s) decay events produced in a proton-beam experiment, using the BCL collaboration's detector system with high precision.

String theory's T-duality exhibits a novel feature, its algebraic nature being rooted in tensor products of continuous-trace algebras.  We discover a precise mathematical characterization of the classical objects that represent this non-geometric duality phenomenon.  Characterized by a specific symmetry algebra and an associated quadratic form, these objects demonstrate a quantized, twisted interpretation of T-duality's geometric formulation.  Upon further examination of this formulation, we determine that a continuous trace algebra plays a crucial role in facilitating T-duality within a string theory context.  Consequently, we identify a criterion for the existence of classical T-duals in T-fibrations.  Our analysis confirms that Hilbert class T-duals meet this criterion, whereas multi-valued moduli do not.  While the latter's associated continuous trace algebras possess classical T-duals, their significance within T-fibrations remains an area of potential future exploration.

Current imitative learning approaches typically rely on exemplary demonstrations, but these can be costly and time-consuming to obtain in practice. In an effort to address this limitation, we introduce Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), a novel training method that leverages a agent's partnership with its own avatars to learn tasks. In our CoIL framework, one agent is trained as a coach by collecting experience, while a second agent, the trainee agent, converts this knowledge into its own policy. CoIL enables i) the coach agent to adapt its strategy according to its own characteristics and ii) knowledge transfer between partner agents. As a result, the trainee agent can be as different as possible from its coach, allowing for effective training in cooperative settings. We demonstrate the CoIL approach in a complex multi-goal Minecraft environment and show its superiority over traditional imitative learning methods that are limited by available exemplary demonstrations.

We derive an asymptotic expression for the probability of sequence errors in a sequential decoder utilizing polar codes, under the assumption of binary symmetric channel decoding. By selecting the polarized cutoff rate as the bias value, we show that the error probability decreases exponentially with codeword length, for a fixed average number of decoding operations per codeword, that is, for 0 < R < R_p, where R is the codeword rate and R_p is the cutoff rate. This finding contrasts previous results, which demonstrated exponential error rate reduction, for bijective mappings, such as R = R_p in practical polar codes, or R < I_w in finite fields with weight-based mappings. We further demonstrate, through the application of the delta-method in probability and statistics, that we can approximate the error probability using the Q-function, and that this approximation is valid for codeword sizes, for fixed decoding complexity, when R is strictly less than R_p, or when R approaches R_p as the codeword size increases. We illustrate, through the simulation of the LDPM decoder, that our theory provides a useful and accurate guide for the performance and complexity trade-offs in designing practical polar codes.

This research introduces a computer vision approach to follow a hand while it interacts with an object in real-time, even when the object enters the frame or creates obstructions. This technique models hands as two separate points and assigns each finger its corresponding direction to enhance tracking accuracy and create a more comprehensive hand representation. To successfully track hands and objects in these scenarios, the system employs a unique "obstruction map," generated from the current object's position, to adjust the hand tracker's influence range and prevent it from deviating when the hand interacts with the object. The output from this hand tracker functions as a "force" that guides a smoother object tracker, allowing the system to track objects close to the hand without entering the interaction zone. This region is treated as an exception. The system's performance was tested through various experiments involving hands interacting with obstructions and a simulated game where users tracked a ball using their hand's movement, with the system proving effective and easy to integrate into applications that require force or velocity-based tracking.

In 1992, R. Ellis classifies reduced groups in his book "Topological Groups and Quantitative Structures." Building on his work, the author of the present paper continues to explore this classification, which was initially undertaken by D. W. Henderson in 1992. Henderson classifies a specific set of reduced groups over a finite topological field containing two elements, $\mathbb{Q}_2$. The current building on his findings by identifying the groups that are homeomorphic over a specific field. The result confirms that these reduced groups consist of the topological group of real numbers and five specific groups of $p$-adic integers.

A novel, sensor-level model calibration approach is introduced in this research, 
utilizing an eye-hand system with depth camera and robot tools as the subject, 
without requiring an external device. The subject's end-effector pose is tracked 
in real-time, thanks to the hand-eye system calibration process. The approach is 
calibrated using the hand-eye system calibration method, allowing for accurate 
pose estimation of the external target. Subsequently, a subject-specific 
calibration is performed, enabling robust and precise pose estimation for the 
subject, even when they hold tools or end-effectors in real-time applications.

Choosing the correct analysis unit for studying network interference in experiments is crucial. Several studies have found conflicting results when different analysis units are tested. We identify and solve this problem by utilizing modern insights from both diffusion models and network remapping techniques. Through network remapping, we can estimate the scope and direction of potential spillover effects for each network focal unit. Network focal units exhibiting distinct remap patterns and those with spillover on remapped network units are identified and separated, allowing researchers to make informed decisions about the most suitable analysis unit. Using a simulation of a real study, we demonstrate that the choice of network focal unit can significantly impact experimental findings and provide a tool for determining the network focal unit prior to data collection.

The formation, thermal equilibrium, and thermal evolution of a neutron star core are analyzed, considering cooling effects from dark matter (DM) self-annihilation and by-neutrino emission resulting from DM self-annihilation and from excited nuclei. It is observed that depending on neutron star thermal evolution data, self-annihilating dark matter could be present with a cross-section of $10^{-23}$ to $10^{-22}$ cm$^3$/s, resulting in cooling cross-sections of $10^{-23}$ to $10^{-21}$ cm$^2$/MeV$^5$ for excited nuclei. Consequently, self-annihilating dark matter could exist near the neutron star's production site with a density approximately $10^9$ times higher than local dark matter density in the galaxy, $0.37$ GeV/cm$^3$, leading to potentially significant direct or indirect DM detection signals on Earth.

Publicly available galaxy surveys rely on accurate galaxy shape calculations for their key findings, such as cosmological conclusions from weak-lensing analyses. Most open-access catalogues lack this information, forcing researchers to develop their own estimates using in-house pipelines. In-house development often poses challenges due to inconsistent results and an lack of transparency. To alleviate this issue, we introduce ShapePipe, a user-friendly gallery application that facilitates collaboration and shared code utilization among researchers with varying levels of in-house coding expertise. By consolidating the capabilities of six existing galleries under a unified interface, we ensure that researchers have consistent evaluations of galaxy shapes, errors, and higher-order moments. We invite the research community to download ShapePipe from github.com/AstroDes/ShapePipe and contribute to its ongoing development.

We establish a connection between solutions to Veech's discrete 2-circle problem and the geodesic flow on modified versions of surfaces with geodesic flows. Furthermore, we calculate the frequency with which closed orbits in the modified surfaces split to form closed orbits in the original surface, effectively solving the Veech version of the Hausdorff measure issue for surfaces exhibiting geodesic flows.

We establish a criterion for k-rationality in hypersurfaces, building upon T. Sano's work on minimal exponents, which refines certain results by B. Kahn. Our finding demonstrates that a hypersurface is k-rational if and only if it has a certain minimal exponent that does not exceed a specific value. This minimal exponent can be expressed as an intersection number involving the hypersurface and a exceptional divisor on a minimal resolution.

We investigate spin chain behavior in the quantum pinwheel compound [Cu(pz)_2(2-HOpy)_2](PF_6)_2 (CP2P), which contains a chain of copper ions linked by hydrogen bonds. In CP2P, the transverse components of spin interactions are naturally around 1% of longitudinal interactions. By applying magnetic fields, we can control the ratio of these components. Using NMR and ESR techniques, we observe that spin fluctuations along the chain are significantly altered near a specific magnetic field orientation, where a chain-like state emerges. Notably, our findings reveal that quantum correlations among spins are not limited to nearest neighbors. Instead, we observed that spins separated by up to seven bonds along the chain can exhibit significant mutual entanglement. Furthermore, we discovered that even after the chain exits its ground state, certain pairs of spins can remain entangled through a phase transition associated with a different ground state.

We examine the $\alpha$-Model-Independent Scenario as a prototype for addressing the
hierarchy and vacuum stability challenges within the context of next-toMinimal
Standard Model. The $\alpha$MSM model expands the standard model by introducing two singlet scalars, one of which acquires a complex vacuum expectation value, while its real component is integrated out. Due to the incorporation of two scalars and a fermion, the strong CP problem is resolved, aligning with one of the primary objectives of many beyond standard model theories, while the contribution to vacuum stability is also analyzed. A range of parameters is explored to establish constraints, utilizing a combination of requirements from the Higgs sector, perturbativity, and various experimental, cosmological and phenomenological considerations. Ultimately, the $\alpha$MSM model demonstrates the ability to resolve the strong CP problem, provide an explanation for dark matter and address the vacuum stability problem, while adhering to existing experimental constraints.

Quantic has introduced an innovative quantum circuit simulator that efficiently combines the benefits of Fock, Stokes, and Clifford and T basis representations to accurately calculate classical observables from quantum computations as well as probability distributions from quantum circuits consisting of Clifford and T gates. By extending the work of Haah, Klowden, Preskill, and Shenker, we quantify and enhance the influence of non-C Clifford and T gate components, demonstrating that even minimal deviations can drastically increase the difficulty of simulation. This discovery provides a novel, practical approach to simulation with improved scalability.

This study, based on the Tsallis holographic dark energy model, is founded on the assumption that dark energy density derives from a maximum energy scale defined by the Hubble radius, and its parameters can be determined through the Tsallis statistical distribution's characteristics. The research, however, has faced criticism, and a correction is proposed. By treating the correction scale, $1/\Lambda$, as both the model's and a maximum energy scale, $\Lambda$, it is suggested that the two are interactively linked. As a result, the state equation, $w$, of the model is found, and its evolution over time is examined within an flat $w$ and dynamical $w$ model. Various, theoretically, and physically, upper bounds for the coupling parameter, $\xi$, are derived. Various, theoretically, and physically, upper bounds for the coupling parameter, $\xi$, are derived. Various, theoretically, and physically, upper bounds for the coupling parameter, $\xi$, are derived

The 4-m 21-dm Large Sky Area Multi-object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope's time-domain survey, which began in 2021, covered a vast 25,000 square degree area of the sky. Initially, the team identified nearly 1,500 variable stars in the target fields by combining spectroscopic and astrometric data. Furthermore, the team compiled a catalog of binary candidates showing significant changes in velocity, encompassing 2,114 objects. Observations of the target fields took place eight times a year, spanning a 30-day window around each epoch, to monitor the nightly variations of the targets. With an exposure time of about 30 seconds per target, the team was able to gather high-quality near-infrared light curves for their targets. Here, we outline the methodology and data processing strategies employed in the LAMOST TDS. Initial analyses of the data have been made and the resulting catalogs are made available on the LAMOST data public website for everyone to access.

The randomness provided by a true random number generator (TRNG) is highly valued, but conventional TRNG designs suffer from slow operation speeds and high energy consumption. In an effort to overcome these limitations, we present a novel, hardware-based TRNG called TuRaN, which utilizes a 10-GHz 65-nm CMOS circuit consisting of a ring oscillator, an inverter, and an input combination logic gate to generate random bits. These random numbers are then verified using a battery of statistical tests. Notably, our analysis of the TRNN's output shows that a chain of 15 ring oscillators yields random-bit streams that are of superior quality. When compared to a state-of-the-art TRNN design published in 2018, our analysis indicates that the proposed TRNN design achieves a 3.5x higher throughput (64 Gbps) and a 2.4x lower energy consumption. The project was successfully demonstrated in a 0.004-mm^2 1-W commercial off-the-shelf CPU, where the random numbers generated were found to be secure against the FIPS standard attack.

A novel on/off resistive switch capable of storing binary data through quantum confinement is presented, operated based on the Pauli exclusion principle. A MOS capacitor with a single-electron tunneling gate and a single-electron tunneling bit as a gate oxide offers the advantage of efficient writing and stable retention of information. A simulation model has been developed to optimize the design and achieve a high on/off current ratio of around 10^4 at an low operating voltage of approximately 0.1 V. This innovative design opens the door for the efficient and sustainable expansion of computational systems.

The application of Feynman integrand causal representations has proven beneficial in massless one-loop computations due to its capacity to reflect loop topology through the factorization properties of singularities. Although this notion is applicable to all loops, its utility has been largely confined to one-loop computations until now. Using this representation in multi-loop computations presents several challenges, including a discrepancy between causal factors and propagators, the absence of factors corresponding to loops, and the coexistence of causal factors and propagators. Despite these hurdles, the author successfully addresses these issues and achieves a fully causal representation for two-loop diagrams with a quadrilateral graph. This new approach not only confirms the validity of the causal representation across multiple loops but also signifies a novel method for computing Feynman integrals in multi-loop diagrams, ultimately revealing a link between the causal representation and scalar invariants.

This study examines the connection between the Green functions and spectral measures of quantum walks. Green functions are analyzed using their asymptotic characteristics and this relationship enables a transition from discrete to continuous time. Such continuous-time limits can serve as valuable reference points or benchmark models. For instance, this limit process has been utilized to investigate the near-deterministic quantum walk on the complete graph.

Researchers have used star data to determine that chiral and color symmetry in quark phase have distinctive features in hybrid stars. In conjunction with constraints from star mass and pressure, mass constraints from protontons and hyperons in stars help to narrow down the possible features of quark phase. By applying the quark MIT bag model and quark phase with phase transition via Gibbs thermodynamics, hybrid star mass and radius data reveal the feasibility of Color Charge Mixture Model (CCCM) and complete chiral symmetry restoration. Resulting mass constraints indicate that maximum mass stars contain a significant fraction of deconfined quark matter. With minimal constraints on quark phase features, up to 60% of hybrid star mass could be deconfined quark matter. In case of phase transition via Gibbs thermodynamics, however, up to 85% could be deconfined quark matter, indicating a significant role of phase transition in hybrid stars and thus, features of quark phase are crucial in understanding star composition.

We are investigating an optomechanical system that involves an $q$-deformed optical mode and a tunneling coupling between two potential wells. The system's ability to produce exceptional points is influenced by tunneling and optomechanical coupling in a specific way. Additionally, we are exploring the effects of tunneling and coupling on the Q-function and P-function for the system. Furthermore, we are examining how tuning tunneling and coupling strengths impacts the P-function and radiated probe field.

A detailed comparison between the "scissors mode" in even-even and odd-odd nuclei has been performed within the cranking approximation of the Interacting Shell Model. The study found that nuclei with R-positive transition characteristics exhibit electromagnetic transition strengths significantly stronger than those associated with R-negative transitions. The analysis also considered the electric quadrupole transitions involving states with angular momentum l=1 and magnetic quantum numbers |k|=1, 1 in nuclei such as $^{90}$Zr, $^{98}$Zr, $^{94}$Mo, $^{96}$Mo, $^{102}$Ru, and $^{106}$Ru. The investigation reveals that R-negative states in even-even nuclei are not associated with scissors modes, but rather represent independent shape isomers possessing an anisotropic shape with an R-negative quantum number property.

This investigation examines the phenomenon of thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition through a comprehensive first-principles study. Employing model systems, our analysis delves into how electronic, optical, and transport properties are influenced by a material's thickness in two- and three-dimensional systems. Furthermore, our analysis also considers collective excitations and their impact on the material's electrical conduction. Notably, our data aligns with recent experimental findings on thin-film black phosphorus, and it also provides a thorough comparison of electronic and optical properties of black phosphorus across different thicknesses.

In our comprehensive theoretical study of laser-cooled atomic or molecular groups,
we establish a theoretical framework capable of accurately predicting nearly any
almost any feature in a distribution with abrupt changes and lowst values,
demonstrating that these discontinuities are linked to the highst powers in a series
expansion. This research reveals that the presence of lowst values is tied to series
convergence. To our knowledge, this is the first time such a thorough analysis has been
conducted. We then apply our approach to predict, in particular, the influence of
photons rebounding off a mirror on flat optical lattices, as well a theoretical
demonstration of a new, highly accurate statistical model - the negative binomial
distribution. Notably, by utilizing features from our theoretical analysis, we are able
to simplify and streamline this complex statistical model. This provides an extensive
set of analytical predictions that can be experimentally tested, particularly in
scenarios where series convergence is certain. This research also guides theoretical
analyses by identifying key factors - series convergence and the presence of lowst values
- that must be met for a statistical model to be applicable in theory and in practice.

In our study, we analyzed monthly data from 2020 and the first half of 2021, focusing on cryptocurrency trading transactions sourced from CryptoCompare. We constructed a trading network by treating each cryptocurrency as a node and the top 10 most traded currency pairs as edges, with edge weights determined by their trading frequencies. We investigated the temporal evolution of this network's topological structure, specifically its small-world and scale-free properties. We observed a notable increase in the network's complexity, connectedness, and centralization during the period from March to June 2021, which we attributed to the surge in cryptocurrency trading transactions, with a total of 132.5 billion transactions recorded in the first half of 2021.

A quantum mechanical analysis of the $H^+$ transfer between a sulphuric acid molecule and water cluster has been conducted. The study focused on how quantum zero-point movements and the thermal vibrations of the $OH_2$ and $HSO_4^-$ groups affect proton transfer are key aspects of this investigation. For the purpose of this study, the active part of the system was modeled using an ab initio method, while its interaction with the surrounding environment was simulated through a way to quantify this ab initio system's movement relative to the environment's classical mean position and its fluctuation measure. The calculated results show that the environment's quantum behavior significantly affects the proton transfer, and the activation barrier for proton transfer is reduced by approximately 10-15% compared to its classical counterpart. Additionally, the study found that the environment's zero-point movements of the $HSO_4^-$ group have very little effect on the barrier, while the zero-point movements of the $OH_2$ group increase the barrier. Furthermore, the study observed that the long-range thermal vibrations of the $HSO_4^-$ group actually decrease the barrier in this system.

Consider operators from a metric space to itself, with the constraint that they do not increase the distance between any pair of points, while also maintaining invariance with respect to a group of transformations. Under the uniform norm and compact-open topology, the set of such operators can be isometrically and compactly embedded within the product space of all possible mappings from a complete metric space to itself. A key finding reveals that the set of equivariant non-expansive maps forms a closed subset within this product space. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the group of transformations acting as symmetries has a limited influence on the equivariant non-expansive maps, allowing for the equivariant maps between certain spaces to be identified as those that maintain specific functions and a spatial correspondence that preserves distances. This includes embeddings where the transforming group consists of isometries.

A comprehensive statistical analysis is conducted for a single particle in a constant temperature field. A comprehensive set of transport coefficients and relations between them and transport processes is presented. All relevant equations are derived in this analysis. Key findings show that the Einstein relation and flux expression are not applicable for systems with a varying temperature profile, and transport processes are interconnected and interdependent. Consequently, characterizing a system by its mobility, diffusivity, or other conventional transport parameters and processes is not feasible.

A critical problem in deep learning model training is implicit model regularization, 
which significantly affects model performance despite its mechanism remaining poorly 
understood. In this research, we investigate how regularization techniques such as 
parameter norm regularization affect the complexity of trained models through implicit 
regularization. By analyzing these mechanisms, we've discovered a new form of 
implicit model regularization, complexity regularization, through the development 
of several theoretical results. It's been shown that training heurics like parameter 
regularization control a trained model's complexity by minimizing its VC-dimension and 
Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension, respectively. Our analysis also provides a 
quantitative measure of the complexity reduction a trained model achieves and an 
explanation as to why certain models generalize better than others. These findings 
have led us to view implicit regularization as a vital component of successful deep 
learning and proposed complexity regularization as a universal approach for 
implementing implicit regularization in deep learning tasks.

This study presents a combined analysis of the D*s(2380)+ decays to K_A(504)+ π(0) and K̄_A(504)- π(+), which allow for a detailed investigation of these D*s transitions and potential new D*s resonances. By employing an advanced unbinned maximum likelihood fit technique, we can calculate precise background yields and signal parameters, ultimately achieving better statistical accuracy in determining effective masses or signal yields. Our method demonstrates a considerable improvement in statistical precision over the most advanced numerical methods, with differences as high as 30% for background mass determinations. The results also show varying degrees of enhancement in statistical precision for phyical parameters, odds ratios, and signal yields, with improvements of up to 20%, up to 15%, and up to 13% respectively. All analyses were carried out using ROOT version 6.08.

The effectiveness of Data augmentation and extended pre-training datasets have been demonstrated in NLP tasks, particularly in language model pre-training. This study investigates whether these techniques can be beneficial in training smaller models on labeled datasets, specifically for automated essay grading. Two types of data augmentation techniques were implemented: sentence shuffling and synonym replacement. These techniques were applied to student essays in the Open Domain NLP Challenge 2021. The results revealed that shuffling significantly improved the performance of all supervised models, while synonym replacement was inconsistent. Notably, the use of augmented data had a more pronounced effect on models trained with a full dataset compared to those trained with a subset. The augmented data had a more significant impact on regression tasks than on categorization tasks.

We investigate methods for assessing parameters in models based on marginal independence structures, a broader category that encompasses Markov random fields and marginal independence models. This paper delves into two key estimation techniques, maximum likelihood and method of moments, and establishes existence, consistency, and asymptotic normality results for our proposed estimators. These mathematical groundings are then applied to establish existence, consistency, and asymptotic normality results for specific models including latent variable models with independent latent distributions and latent variable models with independent latent and observed distributions.

The distribution of opportunities within a society is not merely an ethical concern but an economic one as well, as opportunities today influence the socio-economic structure of future generations. This study presents a two-period economic model that incorporates intergenerational transfers and examines the deterministic equilibrium. We demonstrate the existence of a'spectrum of equilibria,' wherein some individuals in the second period receive opportunities while others do not. Furthermore, our study shows that this opportunity distribution can be transferred to the third period, potentially altering its composition in each subsequent period. Consequently, our findings imply that opportunities should be viewed as a non-renewable resource, underscoring the importance of equalizing opportunities to prevent a systemic institutionalization of inequalities.

According to current understanding, wave functions of the same type of particle must have a specific factor, based on the permutation of their coordinates, which is determined by the spin of the particles. Spin-1/2 fermions produce a -1 factor, while bosons with integer spin produce a +1 factor. However, this convention has a significant issue, as it prevents certain physical processes involving multiple identical particles, such as a pair of electrons interacting to produce a pair of photons, from occurring at all under specific conditions due to symmetry requirements. To resolve this problem, a new factor, involving the sum of the permuted particle coordinates, has been proposed to make some of these processes possible and potentially reopen the possibility for fractional statistics in nature.

Cryptocurrency like Monero boasts strong security features, but its transaction verification process takes a long time due to complex cryptographic techniques, specifically ring signatures and Groesterslign Zero-knowledge proofs. Our proposed Delegated RingCT approach enhances efficiency by using a trusted delegation model, shifting some verification workload to a more scalable delegation layer. This method can easily be applied to ring signatures and is integrated with Monero's existing technology in a way that maintains its original security level, potentially providing an ideal solution for cryptocurrency transactions in terms of verification speed and scalability.

For any constant epsilon greater than zero, this research transforms reductions between approximate solvers of linear systems into circuit complexity transformations. Specifically, it shows that an approximate solver capable of handling systems with coefficients in a subset of the complex numbers and rank at most r can be converted into a circuit that solves a system approximately, with rank limited to |r|/3, using only slightly more computational resources. This computational cost increase does not exceed a factor of five times logarithmic of r and seven times logarithmic of the problem size n. Furthermore, this computational resource requirement can be significantly reduced to O(log log r) + O(log n) when considering precomputation. As a direct result, this circuit-based reduction yields circuit-amplitude reduction properties. This circuit-amplitude reduction implies that, regardless of the order of certain linear systems, their circuit complexity classes exhibit complete relationships. Additionally, this circuit-based reduction yields a substantial circuit size reduction property, which implies that certain circuit sizes are required to approximately solve linear systems. This circuit size reduction property also leads to a substantial circuit depth reduction property, which reveals certain circuit depth requirements for approximate solver transformations. This depth reduction is particularly remarkable, which means that, to transform one approximate solver into another, it is not necessary to interact between multiple circuit layers, but only a constant number of layers are required. This constant value is limited to at most five. Finally, this result is complemented by an algorithm that directly produces an approximate solver with comparable circuit depth.

The calculated cross-sections are 6.29 nb for WWW and 14.16 pb for WWZ, with minimal statistical and systematic uncertainties. Cross-section measurements are determined to be 5.96 nb for WWW and 14.16 pb for WWZ, with deviations from predicted standard model cross-sections. The last two decades have seen significant growth in Natural Language Processing for Hebrew. This field's advancement is largely attributed to high-quality data sets, which have lagged behind English resources. Research in Hebrew NLP has been supported by two UD treebanks, UTSE and Hebreu. These contributed to significant breakthroughs; however, their limitations became apparent as new applications grew. A new data set, UDHebrew, is developed to over come these shortcomings and further improve NLP results. By offering a well-tested dataset with a rich resource of pre-trained models, UDHebrew enables the development of more versatile and precise Hebrew language tools. Evaluation of UDHebrew shows remarkable progress, with state-of-the-art models achieving 87.12% and 85.74% accuracy on morphological and word level tasks, respectively. This work details the construction and evaluation of UDHebrew and its effects on Hebrew NLP advancements.

J. Bourgain established in his thesis that any epsilon-isometric reduction of the unit ball of the ell_p space can be achieved through a nonlinear process, specifically by applying a distance-preserving transformation followed by a linear projection. The question arises as to which types of ell_p spaces, parameterized by p values between 1 and infinity, can be reduced via such linear operators? The research of our group shows that these ell_p spaces exhibit a distinct property, exhibiting resistance to epsilon-isometric dimension reduction via linear operators for any p value other than 2. The proof is rooted in demonstrating that any linear map, preserving most distances within the ell_p unit ball, must also maintain a considerable amount of structure within the original space. By applying relevant lemmas from the John and von Neumann theories, it can be deduced that such linear maps correspond to nearly isometric transformations in the original space and nearly isometric compressions of high-dimensional convex bodies. The application of these principles confirms that almost all ell_p spaces (for p values other than 2) cannot be reduced via linear operators while maintaining epsilon-isometry.

Computer models of plasticity in solid mechanics are widely recognized for their complex, multi-scale characteristics. Described using the ODE framework, their parameters exhibit time-varying behavior, necessitating frequent re-estimation. From a constitutive modeling perspective, this presents an analogous challenge to the artificial neural network problem of re-learning previously learned patterns without erasing previously acquired knowledge, which in turn necessitates a novel approach to learning that accommodates its artificial neural network foundations. This work introduces a continuous learning method that enables sequential learning from data sets describing distinct instances of history-dependent plasticity behavior. It achieves this by integrating multi-task continuous optimization of the evolving plasticity parameters and the gradual refinement of their underlying physical properties. As a practical result, this approach facilitates the sequential learning of such parameters and their constitutive model and their subsequent transfer to entirely new problems. To demonstrate the practical viability of this approach, we applied it to the successive learning of multiple problems from data sets describing problems of history-dependent plasticity behavior, which included a numerical simulation and experiments on two materials exhibiting properties of visco-elastic plasticity and another material exhibiting characteristics of kinematic hardening.

The performance of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes when transmitted over a binary erasure channel is analyzed. Based on previous research by Lelievre et al. (2007), which considered channel erasure probabilities below a certain threshold and employed the standard belief propagation decoding algorithm, this research extends its findings to include probabilities above the threshold. In this scenario, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoding algorithm is employed. LDPC codes with degree-degree correlation are generated using three distinct degree degree correlation distributions. The impact of these distributions on the codes' erasure and bit error rates is then evaluated.

This paper proposes the Multi-player Optimal Control Scheme for Modepiecewise Polyhedral Safe Formation (SL-MPSF) to guarantee safe operation for linear systems under bounded disturbances. Unlike existing formation safety approaches, SL-MPSF does not rely on conservative distance guarantees. Instead, it optimizes safe formation trajectories in real-time while minimizing a cost function, thus reducing unnecessary restrictions. We validate the SL-MPSF scheme through theoretical proofs of safety and optimality, as well as through simulation examples showcasing its effectiveness.

We propose a theoretical attack on the quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol that uses a combination of vacuum and weak decoy states. This proposed attack, which cannot be triggered, allows an external party to significantly interfere with the QKD process without being detected. In a specific experiment, our proposed attack was successful in reducing the key generation rate by up to 97.3% and increasing the QBER by as much as 17.1 percentage points. Furthermore, when we modified our proposed attack to be more conservative, we observed a direct relationship between the size of the attack and the security measures implemented by the manufacturers of commercial QKD systems.

There has been a rapid increase in the development of natural language generation models, leading to the widespread adoption of in-context learning for their applications. In a study on the relationship between language modeling and in-context learning, we found that models with low perplexity often perform well in few-shot in-context learning tasks. Despite this observation, there are significant challenges in consistently selecting the most effective model parameters and cache warm-up issues that affect model performance during inference. In order to gain insight into the correlation between language modeling and in-context learning, we conducted a more thorough systematic analysis of the relationship. Our initial experiment focused on comparing the performance of different models, including the OpenAI text-davinci models, on few-shot in-context learning tasks, and we found that low perplexity models performed better in these tasks. However, different best-fitting open-source models exhibited inconsistent results, suggesting that perplexity may not be a universal guarantee for in-context learning success. In order to understand the basis for the initial observation, we conducted a more detailed investigation of the correlation between language modeling and in-context learning tasks, including in-context learning calibration. Our analysis focused on identifying factors such as the quality of the training corpus, model parameterization, and the impact of cache warm-up on in-context learning performance. We've studied the effect of anisotropic thermal conduction on the inversion of an entropy profile in galaxy clusters. By analyzing real-world data from angular diameter distance measurements, we've found that conduction could explain some observed deviations from predicted galaxy cluster mass-temperature relations. Our research indicates that cold gas growth due to conduction is significantly slower than previously observed, typically peaking at redshift about 0.6. However, we've discovered that this growth is highly sensitive to the slope of the entropy profile's core, peaking as late as redshift about 0.8 in some cases. We've also found that in about 50% of cases, cold gas actually shrinks over time, rather than peaking at zero redshift. This suggests that anisotropic heat conduction might not fully explain the observed trends in galaxy clusters.

The Standard Model predicts a significant disparity between beauty baryons and their antiparticles in the context of direct CP violation, which offers a valuable platform for exploring CP-violating phenomena and a potential source of CP-violation in the Standard Model. Recent advances in direct CP-violation studies on beauty baryons and charm systems, driven by the LHCb experiment, are capable of detecting even the smallest deviations from the Standard Model predictions. This review examines the current status of direct CP-violation studies in beauty and charm baryons, highlighting discrepancies from Standard Model predictions.

We have developed fresh insights into the scattering of hard strings by reevaluating T-duality within effective field theory. Our findings indicate that string amplitudes follow the predicted patterns from previous conjectures, specifically showing that these processes lose coherence as energy increases. This conclusion aligns with the concept of string theory's 'fuzzball' model. By leveraging parity and the invariance of momentum in amplitude calculations, we derived constraints that allowed us to further refine the amplitude formulas. Notably, we discovered a newly established relationship between these formulas. Our work also entails deriving a transport equation for the scattering matrix and examining its behavior. Upon direct computation, we found that in the high-energy limit, the rate of change in the scattering matrix tends to zero. We further analyzed the scattering process in this context by leveraging conformal field theory principles and leveraged knowledge of soliton-like solitions within such fields.

This research proposes a novel task offloading model for online sequential data, aiming to optimize edge computing systems with multiple virtual servers. The model is formulated as a Markov decision process, with an adaptive learning algorithm to adjust its parameters over time. This formulation aims to minimize cumulative energy consumption while reducing task execution time. The study further introduces two additional optimization goals, focusing on reducing Power Consumption Performance (PCPP) and Processing Delay Performance (PDP). These metrics evaluate a server's efficiency in processing tasks within edge computing facilities. Utilizing Performance Dissipation (PD) and thermal performance equations, the optimized processing model is presented, followed by a comparison of various offloading strategies. This framework can be applied to various online sequential data tasks, such as task offloading, network registration, and data transmission.

Most speech synthesis models incorporate a duration model, which generates the number of frames for each phoneme, as seen in the FastSpeech system that uses average phoneme lengths. However, this approach lacks the ability to model variations in speech duration resulting from distinct phonemic compositions, such as the difference between transient and steady-state states or transient and transient. Transient phonemes include those with short or non-long vowel durations, while steady-state phonemes have longer, non-short vowel durations. Another factor is phrasing, which classifies phonemes as either belonging to brief phrases with transient phonemes or extended phrases with stable phonemes.

It has been observed that certain sound effects, such as voice onsets, voice declines, voice breaks, and voice ends, are more frequently found in transient phonemes than in steady phonemes. On the other hand, sound effects, such as voice stays, are more commonly found in steady phonemes than in transient phonemes. This suggests that modeling phoneme duration based on these categories as separate categories may provide a more detailed control over these sound effects, compared to modeling phoneme duration based on phonetic content alone.

To investigate this hypothesis, a new system called FSVoice was created, extending the FastSpeech system with an additional dimension of speech representation, which separates transient and steady phonemes into distinct categories. This paper presents a novel, comprehensive method to optimize movement plans for robots with multiple limbs in complex environments by combining joint trajectory optimization with inverse kinematics. Due to the high number of joints, direct optimization is computationally burdensome, so our proposed two-step approach first generates a basic motion plan using simplified position-level optimization, then refines it with precise joint-level optimization for precise collision-free movement. Leveraging the flexibility of symbolic tube control, our method enables efficient staging of tasks, allowing for the simultaneous optimization of multiple robot trajectories. Additionally, we employ conic optimization for precise joint-level planning, resulting in significant performance improvements over traditional methods such as CHOMP and STOMP in terms of planning speed and solution accuracy.

In various applications, there is a necessity to obtain rare, highly resource-intensive quantum states. A quantum technique has been developed to achieve this, allowing one to get around strict limitations on how many times the procedure can be applied, by examining simple questions about the procedure's outcomes. A general analysis was carried out across an extensive range of quantum concepts, examining the trade-offs between achieving maximally resourceful states and errors. Various methods were evaluated through numerical means to assess the method's effectiveness and provide guidance on future use. It was found that in many contexts, fidelity is a valuable tool in quantifying the resource at hand and can ensure noiseless extraction under particular conditions.
