A significant challenge in processing real-world data is protecting the privacy of individuals, especially when analyzing clustering datasets, without incurring excessive costs or diminishing utility. The existing clustering methods, although useful, do not guarantee privacy for individuals and can be costly to implement with differential privacy (DP). To address this concern, we have developed FLVoogd, a private and efficient clustering framework, which allows users to collect only anonymous information from participants and process data outside of their devices, thus minimizing privacy risks. By limiting interactions between agents, FLVoogd reduces communication costs while maintaining a secure environment. Our study shows that, compared to public-key DP-kmeans and key-locker schemes, FLVoogd produces accurate results and ensures a lower DP budget usage, even in an honest-but-curious multi-party computation setting. The experiments also reveal that FLVoogd outperforms existing methods on multiple datasets and personal attributes, especially when dealing with high-dimensional data.

The 2021 autonomous vehicle challenge for city driving showcased remarkable autonomy across a range of scenarios, with a standout focus on sim2real transfer. This concept, involving training models in simulation and deploying them in real-world conditions, underpins most autonomous vehicle developments. However, there has been little research into the underlying causes of varying levels of success in sim2real transfer. This study delves into the issue by analyzing a common technique, domain adaptation, and investigating its effectiveness in over-fitting reduction. The research compares multiple real-world driving datasets, assessing the transferability of domain adaptation methods from simulation to these datasets. The results provide a clear distinction between over- fitting and insufficient learning as barriers to effective sim2real transfer, thereby offering a framework for evaluating model performance in real-world driving situations.

The increasing realism of deepfake media poses significant concerns, particularly the spread of misinformation through manipulated audio and video content. Although previous studies have posed hypothetically manipulated videos as inputs for neural video generation models, no research has explored a practical pipeline for generating videos from real people using adversarial audio source content, which is the primary motivation for our study. We conducted an experiment by using DeepVoice 2 to synthesize speech from real people, which was then input into the generative model RunWay Gemini, which produced videos from real subjects, including everyday actions. The resulting videos were surprising in their content, raising both technical and ethical questions, including a key finding that adversarial content can bypass neural video generation models, producing visually incoherent results. These findings have important implications for the potential misuse of media, especially video, in real-world scenarios, particularly when generating videos from real people. The systemic design of current neural video generation models, which are being developed for their robustness and misalignment for their ultimate purpose, raises additional concerns, as they can produce videos that are semantically incoherent and inconsistent with adversarial audio content. The study's code and pre-trained models are being shared to foster transparent and ethical research in this area.

The size of an Earth's atmosphere is better constrained by our current knowledge. However, an atmosphere smaller than our current one is harder to study due to its atmospheric constraints. We conducted tests using simulated atmospheric profiles of various sizes from temperate planets and found that the tiny atmospheres are composed mainly of heavy, carbon, and nitrogen gases, which are difficult to detect with telescopes. Our current instruments are not capable of determining the composition of these tiny atmospheres, but a future telescope with a chromatic UV grating could do so on rocks larger than Earth. These new observations could provide new insights into the formation and evolution of temperate planets and their atmospheres.

The classic Hopfield network excels at pattern retrieval, yet its learning process is limited to a single step and only applicable to specific cases. A modified McCulloch-Pitts network is proposed as an improvement, allowing the Hopfield network to learn more effectively. Furthermore, this adapted Hopfield network can be applied to denoising and edge detection tasks. It has been specifically tested on two handwritten digit denoising experiments and an image edge detection task.

This paper introduces SceneText, a comprehensive dataset of various text scenes that surpasses existing data resources in both diversity and volume. The proposed SceneText dataset is designed to test the general adaptability of text recognition models, particularly their ability to read unfamiliar text. By training with the SceneText dataset, the recognized increase in on-board character (OBC) accuracy indicates its effectiveness in enhancing on-board training capabilities. The proposed method is evaluated using outstanding open-data models, demonstrating the ability to boost both on-board and general performance. We also introduce a new, extensive benchmark of general text with 100M characters, addressing the data scarcity issue in text recognition. An open-source tool for string synthesis is also developed and introduced.

Isolated system solutions or solution branches can be found using a novel numerical method that incorporates proof-based numbers. By applying Newton's method with validated arithmetic, a parameter-dependent solution branch can be computed segment by segment. Each segment is generated starting from an initial guess that is verified to satisfy the equation, which can be achieved by either solving for a new parameter value or by validating the entire system over a given parameter interval using Stokes' theorem. A novel result has been developed to efficiently find isolated system branches with varying complex parameters. The efficiency of this method is demonstrated using two complex examples, including a model for a fluid dynamics system and the first few branches of a model for a fluid-fluid interface interface. The method demonstrates the first validation of multiple solution branches and their continuation over a defined parameter interval, as well as a demonstration of a model's multiple unstable states over a defined fluid surface.

In the field of quality control, statistical process control methods monitor continuous process data to identify deviations from normal operations. Since data-driven isolation of failure modes emerged in the late 2000s, several state-of-the-art isolation methods have since been developed. However, these methods were designed for standalone applications and were not combined with change point detection methods, which are crucial in quality control. In this research, we integrate change point detection and isolation of failure modes through an iterative process, finding that performance significantly improves in high-dimensional settings and environments with limited computational resources.

Following a recent discovery of a high velocity dwarf galaxy, named Wukong, in the Milky Way's outer halo, research revealed it to be an example of an in-situ accreted structure, distinct from other merged galactic models, and is part of the same object identified as Gaia-Sausage Enceladus, or GSE, based on matching velocities and chemical properties. Furthermore, Wukong, a disk galaxy approximately 3 kiloparsecs in size, exhibited star formation lasting 2 to 3 gigayears. Its outer regions, however, show GSE/Wukong five billion-year-old stellar populations mixing with the Milky Way's disc. Wukong's chemical properties, velocity distribution, and morphological characteristics provide unique insights, differentiating its paleo-galaxy host from GSE's typical characteristics. These findings are significant for understanding paleo-galactic mergers and predicting satellite galaxies' appearance based on M33-like models.

This article examines the homotopy orbit spectrum $(Z[[G]])_{hG}$ for pro-finite groups $G$ and completes a thought initiated by Hill, Hesselholt and Madsen. It demonstrates that this homotopy orbit spectrum is equivalent to the spectrum $Z$ under the condition that $G$ has a pro-finite completion that is a solvable arithmetic group.

Acquiring well annotated data can be costly, making it crucial to minimize this cost while maintaining high performance in machine learning models. Selective labeling focuses on enhancing label quality by leveraging a current model to guide a human annotator's expertise, thereby increasing its effectiveness. This study investigates the benefits of labeling decisions informed by human strategy and learned uncertainty, incorporating these methods into labeling decisions. Furthermore, it explores labeling decisions based on object classes and object details. Ultimately, experimental results demonstrate that integrating these strategies yields object-level labeling accuracies comparable to annotations made by skilled annotators, yet through fewer labels and at a lower cost.

A key area of study in modern condensed matter physics is two-dimensional electronic systems with unique properties at interfaces. One such system is formed when a ferromagnetic material, EuS, is placed in contact with a nonmagnetic semiconductor, InAs. To gain insight into the electronic properties of this interface, researchers employed resonant x-ray photoemission spectroscopy to investigate its core-level core-hole spectroscopy. They discovered that when the binding energy of the 3d core level in Eu matches the valence band energy of InAs, multiple electronic states emerge. Notably, these states are spatially localized and oriented perpendicularly to the interface. Furthermore, researchers observed significant spin polarization of up to 50% in the dispersed valence band states, even exceeding the polarization levels within the interface itself. X-ray magnetic circular dichroism confirmed that the prevalent electronic configuration responsible for the observed states is primarily composed of europium 4f and sulfur 3p states, rather than elemental contributions from indium or arsenic. This discovery provides valuable information about the chemical composition and electronic structure present at the interface of EuS/InAs.

We establish a connection between several principles in second-order arithmetic and descriptive set theory by demonstrating that Borel Wadge determinacy is equivalent to a combination of Borel Hausdorff reduction and Borel Hausdorff well-ordering within the framework of second-order arithmetic.

Model compression plays a crucial role in deploying large-scale image recognition models on devices with limited resources. However, simply reducing the model's complexity may lead to significant performance loss. To address this problem, we introduce ClickTrain, a novel technique that compresses large models while maintaining high accuracy. ClickTrain formulates model compression as a game between compression and the model parameters. We utilize click maps generated by playing the game to remove model parameters. Notably, ClickTrain can be trained end-to-end, allowing the compression process and the model training process to be guided by a gradient-rich signal obtained from the click maps. Our experiments demonstrate that ClickTrain achieves remarkable model compression rates, up to 3200 times, with minimal performance loss. For instance, we converted ResNet50 into a lightweight model that matches MobileNetV2's efficiency, achieving comparable ImageNet accuracy. Furthermore, ClickTrain can be applied to three different computer vision datasets, including CVPR, IJCAI, and ECAI, and obtains state-of-the-art results in computer vision model abstraction. When used for IAB architecture design, ClickTrain outperforms traditional pruning techniques by allowing the creation of a lightweight model with near-original accuracy. Finally, ClickTrain can be combined with other compression techniques for even greater model efficiency.

This study presents a substructural modal logic framework derived from the structural decomposition of sequents, incorporating both multiple-conclusion sequents and the full spectrum of modalities (E, D, T, B, S4, B). By establishing four distinct logical systems, we derive TKB, KTB, KB and B4 as specific instances. To visualize the structure of these new logics, we create four four-dimensional logical graphs, enabling the demonstration of complex logical relationships, including a non-standard inference path from B to D and further back to E within TKB.

The multi-messenger field is defined by the concurrent detection of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation originating from neutron star mergers, a phenomenon that is set to revolutionize our knowledge of the universe. The upcoming generation of multi-bandequipment, including the James Webb Space Telescope and networked gravitational observatories, will significantly improve our capacity to identify the events that drive this new discipline. To comprehensively study these events, a unified database of simulated electromagnetic signals from neutron star mergers needs to be created and made available, allowing researchers to assess the observational potential for each neutron star merger signal. The coexistence of co-incident gravitational and electromagnetic radiation will enable researchers to gain valuable insights into the complex processes that shape the universe, and the creation of the database will facilitate the assessment of the observational potential for each of these events.

The detection of the ultra-short orbit planet TOI-5542b using the TESS satellite presents an intriguing case study, as its host star is an unusually fast rotator for a G-type star. To gather more comprehensive data, we gathered high-quality spectroscopic data from multiple facilities and combined it to precisely measure the star's mass and radius. Our analysis indicates that TOI-5542b is a gas-rich planet with a mass approximately 0.81 times that of Jupiter and a radius around 1.2 times that of Jupiter. Its equilibrium temperature is an scorching 360 K, and if its atmospheric composition were similar to that of Jupiter, its overall mass would have to be 1.5 times greater to maintain thermal equilibrium. Consequently, TOI-5542b is most likely in a hydrodynamic atmospheric escape state, and its atmosphere would be hydrogen/helium dominated with heavier elements providing minimal contrast. Although TOI-5542b's atmospheric escape might not be detectable with current instruments, future atmospheric observations using JWST could start exploring the boundary between atmospheric escape and quiescence.

We tackle a challenging problem of finding the optimal policy for large-scale operational strategies using the min-max deviation robust stochastic programming framework. This involves optimizing policy parameters to minimize policy costs under various probability distributions with unknown means. A sampling-based primal-dual algorithm is proposed to tackle this problem, incorporating dual certificates from probability distributions with unknown means. The method utilizes primal-dual estimates to minimize regret in an associated empirical problem. The proposed algorithm exhibits a linear rate of convergence with an analytically determined convergence rate. The effectiveness of this algorithm is illustrated through a range of numerical experiments.

This research targets the complex mathematical symbol recognition task, which involves a substantial number of categories. Traditional approaches often struggle with this challenge due to the need for a large, memory-intensive training process and the generation of over-fitted one-hot encoded labels. To address this problem, we introduce a novel non-learning-based kNN classifier that effectively handles this problem without the drawbacks associated with traditional machine learning methods. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple mathematical symbol datasets, and the accompanying code and datasets can be found at https://github.com/ashleyfeng97/MathSymbolRecognition.

Using a representation of quantum affine algebras, we investigate the behavior of instanton moduli spaces from the perspective of the nascent quantum harmonic oscillator. This mathematical model builds on the Chern-Simons gauge theory on a 3-manifold that is a connected sum of $K$ copies of the three-dimensional torus. We calculate the quantum dimensions of the relevant instanton moduli spaces as the large $K$ limit approaches a BPS state count with exponential growth. Notably, the base and exponent of this exponential are expressed in terms of the Chern-Simons level $K$ and a dimensionless parameter derived from the torus's complex structure. We demonstrate that the BPS state count exhibits periodic oscillations as the parameter's magnitude increases, with amplitudes that decrease factorially with each period. We also derive an exact formula for the first-order periodic correction in terms of partition numbers.

In this study, we investigate the average case scenario of predicting epidemic spreading on complex networks, where some nodes are unknown. We demonstrate that the bridgeness of a network significantly influences the predictability of epidemic spreading, particularly for models that don't involve randomness. Furthermore, we investigate how adding random nodes and links to a network affects the predictability of different epidemic models, including SIR and BA models. Our findings show that adding random nodes without links decreases predictability, while adding links with random nodes increases it.

In the context of reinforcement learning, achieving safety constraints is a major challenge, particularly as these constraints can drastically limit the range of actions an agent can take, potentially causing it to prioritize short-term safety over long-term goals. Furthermore, collecting sufficient demonstration data to train a robust and compliant agent can be a time-consuming process. This research introduces a novel, data-driven approach to training compliant agents by optimizing the reward function in a latent space. By transforming the agent's policy to comply with safety constraints instead, this method can training agents that are not only compliant with the established safety rules but also align with the desired behavior of safe agents, using a pre-defined action mask. This approach was evaluated using a multi-agent version of the classic grid world game of capture the flag. The results showed training a compliant agent using this method yielded significant improvements when paired with a learning-based agent. This research also explores how action masking can be used to train compliant agents using a variety of reward functions without requiring precise alignment with the safe agent's objectives. This can lead to a more robust agent that is not only compliant with the established safety rules but also aligns with the desired behavior of safe agents, using a preference-based alignment method.

A novel approach to identifying twin primes is presented, a long-standing challenge known as the twin prime conjecture. Our method relies on the use of generators to determine if pairs of primes form a twin prime pair. It has been observed that one member of each twin prime pair is always generated by its partner. This is illustrated with data, such as the pair (11, 13), where 11 has a generator of 13. The proof is straightforward and can be expanded into a theorem. Furthermore, we have developed an algorithm that lists all primes up to a specified limit based on their generators. Notably, this algorithm appears to have no gaps and could potentially provide a proof for the latter part of Polignac's conjecture, which states that for any even number n, there are infinitely many twin prime pairs with a gap of n.

This paper outlines a innovative control architecture designed to streamline the integration of acoustic sensors into mobile platforms' navigation systems. By employing sonar sensors in a localized frame, separated from the global navigation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a simulated M755 mobile platform equipped with sonar sensors strategically positioned around a rectangular obstacle. A sonar-based obstacle avoidance method is also presented to successfully navigate the platform around the obstacle. Moreover, experimental data collected from a real-world testbed validates the proposed strategy.

The most distant known object in the Solar System, Nereid, is primarily distinguished by its exceptionally low albedo and the presence of red-colored surface materials. These characteristics align with those observed in other distant icy bodies. We aim to investigate Nereid's spectral properties and the presence of water ice using Low Resolution Imaging Spectrometer (LIRIS) data from the Jupiter Lunar Observatory (Juno) mission. Specifically, Nereid exhibits a spectral slope that can be attributed to a combination of a red substance with albedo similar to that of tholin, and a substantial contribution from surface water ice. This indicates that Nereid's surface is largely composed of water ice, with a comparable abundance to that of other distant icy bodies and the surfaces of the outer planets.

We have extended affine planes based on the projective line over a ring $R$, to full projective planes and developed a novel representation of the circular order underlying their geometry using a graph structure. Furthermore, we derived the complete order of the extended partial geometric configuration $(P, \mathcal{L}, \mathcal{B})$, where $P$ consists of lines in $R^2$, $\mathcal{L}$ represents those lines intersecting $R^2 \setminus I^2$ in distinct points, and $\mathcal{B}$ consists of all remaining lines. Here, $I$ denotes the unit ideal in $R$.

In this research, the connection between models, cardinal characteristics of the natural numbers, and order types is explored through the lens of Tukey-order. A key outcome of our investigation is an method to demonstrate the implication between various cardinal characteristics, which relies on the presence of a specific model in a lower order than the standard model b being in a lower order than j. To achieve this, the concept of a lower model is first defined, after which two instances are identified, with the first leading to a form of consistent strength higher than the original conjecture and the second providing evidence for strong low - high cardinal characteristic relationships under specific model assumptions.

Combining the well-known pessimism principle with Thompson sampling has not been theoretically established until now, which limits its utility in practical applications, including policy optimization. We address this issue by formally integrating pessimism with Thompson sampling, providing a novel algorithm called Pessimistic Thompson Sampling (PTS). Our research demonstrates that PTS exhibits similar convergence properties as optimistic Thompson Sampling (OTS), but at a lower computational cost. Additionally, we introduce an implementation of PTS with a bounded computational complexity, further facilitating its practical application. Our study also investigates the reasons behind the superior performance of Thompson Sampling when compared to optimistic algorithms in the online learning context. We also present an expanded version ofOTS, known as Optimistic Thompson Sampling with a Bounded Learning Rate (OTSLR), that exhibits bounded regret. OTSLR has been practically demonstrated to offer better results than Thompson Sampling for a range of Dynamic Treatment Regimes (DTR) optimization problems. OTSLR's results also confirm the presence of a non-stationary element in some DTR problems, which explains the relative success of Thompson Sampling. OTSLR's results offer an alternative approach to determining the applicability of Thompson Sampling.

We hold that certain subcategories of finitely generated modules over local Noetherian rings are 'resolving,' implying invariance of associated algebraic K-groups under formal power series ring extensions with integer coefficients. Specifically, the categories of all and maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules are included among these. This finding has significant implications, particularly concerning the invariance of representation stability under such ring extensions.

A method is proposed to connect various quantum configurations through ideal simulations of classical systems, with a focus on the simplest multidimensional geometric model. This enables comparisons of their nonlocal, contextual, and information-theoretic aspects as if they were distinct face-card representations of a single system. The proposal examines context-free simulations of classical systems and raises the question of whether nature can faithfully model such an approach.

In multi-band Hubbard models with exact η-pairing ground states, the strongest pairing occurs at half-filled bands. For bi-band Hubbard models, the strongest pairing happens when all bands are half-filled, which implies that intra-band and inter-band pairs have the same average weight. Contrarily, in multi-band kinetic-models with η-pairing ground states, the strongest inter-band pairing occurs at half-filled active bands while the strongest intra-band hopping occurs at integer filling. Consequently, the average weight of intra-band pairs drops to zero at full filling.

This research investigates p-adic solenoids as a real-number variant and constructs their own versions, also visualizing them in real space. We aim to solve an analogue of a generalized Polya theorem for a-adic solenoids, expressing the function $\phi(x)$ as the sum of specific real-valued functions defined on the interval $[0,1]$, akin to the real case, which can be effectively employed to solve the functional equation.

Cluster analysis of presence-absence data across multiple sites and species 
can be accomplished using various approaches such as multi-variate techniques 
or binary-specific methods, which often create a single cluster solution 
dependent on the chosen method and specified number of clusters. A common 
methodological issue arises from the need to pre-select the number of clusters, 
raising concerns about potential data overfitting. This study investigates the 
utility of consensus network visualisation (as proposed by Densmore and Muir 
(2011)) in selecting the number of clusters for binary data clustering, 
demonstrating that this approach can effectively identify distinct species 
assemblies and community changes without requiring a priori knowledge of the 
number of clusters. A case study, involving data from 42 sites, 31 habitats 
and a diverse range of species, illustrates the application of this 
visualization technique in assessing species distribution patterns and 
habitat shifts over time, thereby facilitating a more informed decision-making 
process for determining the optimal number of clusters.

Salient object detection methods based on deep learning have made significant progress in handling various image types, including RGB and RGB-D images. However, existing approaches have limited generalizability, with models trained on one format struggling to adapt to another. To address this, we introduce a novel deep learning architecture for group learning of multiple modalities, featuring an integrated module to process varying input formats. By merging feature maps from different image types, our unified structure capitalizes on various information channels, enhancing the model's flexibility and adaptability. Moreover, we employ a shared structure for various input formats and a regularization term using self-attention, reducing the number of parameters and optimizing training efficiency. Extensive experiments on several public datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our approach, with detailed investigations of its various components.

This research outlines ABUSIVE-TWEETS, a computational system designed to identify and flag YouTube comments and Twitter posts that violate community standards due to abusive and inappropriate language. Our focus here is on analyzing its performance in detecting abusive content on Twitter and showcasing its effectiveness. ABUSIVE-TWEETS achieved a macro F1 score of 0.862 in our latest evaluation, taking place in the 11th Information Security Research Conference in 2021. While ABUSIVE-TWEETS displays impressive results, there is still space for enhancement, and we hope to refine its capabilities. Additionally, ABUSIVE-TWEETS addresses a critical issue: the pervasive problem of online hate speech and abusive content. With this system, we aim to develop a tool that can efficiently monitor and report such content to relevant online platforms and regulatory bodies.

A novel proof, based on different principles, demonstrates that the set of unrepresentable integers by a given palindromic function $\varphi(n)$ constitutes a sparse collection, with sparse exponent one. This result implies that unrepresentable integers occur infrequently. The paper's findings are particularly relevant to a specific category of non-palindromic numbers, including the longstanding mathematical conjecture regarding which integers can be transformed into palindromes through iteration. By examining this conjecture for various bases, including 2 and other systems, questions arise about the ultimate number of iterations required to achieve a palindrome.

We introduce a novel, linear image reconstruction model that can be customized according to various reordering and reordering inverse schemes, which may be influenced by the imaging system and object characteristics. By separating the data ordering process from the reconstruction algorithm, our model offers flexibility in addressing a range of problems such as limited scan range, non-uniform sampling, and the presence of system-dependent weighting. Furthermore, our model explicitly accounts for different noise types in the data, enabling the development of corresponding regularization algorithms as illustrated in a CT scan with synthetic noise for a phantom image.

This research explores the use of Bayesian Program Learning (BPL) to encode handwritten text styles. By leveraging BPL's ability to represent complex behaviors through compact structures, we demonstrate that generating realistic handwriting styles from as few as five samples is possible. This capability significantly outperforms previous methods that require numerous samples. The proposed model, Handwritten Style Learning (HSL), uses a BPL prior to create a compact decoder for handwritten text. The HSL model is composed of three sequential BPL components, which together form a cohesive structure for generating handwritten text. The HSL model achieves a 3.5x improvement in sample complexity compared to existing techniques and produces sample-level FID scores as low as 147 with just five samples. The HSL model can be replicated using the provided GitHub repository and 142.5 MB model weights.

A new UNM scheme based on Kalkovsky's unification of three-nucleon states is presented. Its goal is to reduce the amount of memory needed to produce a three-nucleon interaction matrix. By unifying three-nucleon bound states and scattering states, the proposed scheme minimizes the number of bound-state matrix elements and demonstrates how to reduce memory requirements regardless of the nucleons involved. As a result, the memory needed to produce three-nucleon interaction matrix elements drops by about 30\% using this scheme. Additionally, both the UNM and inverse UNM processes are described. Their feasibility has been tested using three-nucleon systems with up to 10 partial waves. The UNM scheme can reduce the number of three-nucleon interaction matrix elements by approximately 40\% for all possible three-nucleon systems. These findings have implications for applying UNM to six-nucleon systems.

Quantum electronic phenomena are now widely encountered in modern technology. To effectively leverage these effects, it's crucial to comprehend the underlying quantum relationships between electrical currents and the entanglement principles that govern them. This contribution aims to make such currents' entanglement more accessible to electrical engineers by introducing the correlator method and the von-Neumann density-matrix method. These approaches enable engineers to quantify entanglement between electrical currents and ultimately control it. By applying established criteria such as the Correlation Area Bound, entanglement between electrical currents can be identified. This understanding forms the foundation for designing and controlling circuits harnessing quantum electronic phenomena.

Let's explore the effects of composing functions in the Bergman space, specifically those that map the unit disc onto a bounded, convex shape with smooth edges. We're focusing on composition operators where the composing function, $\varphi$, either has an inverse that's analytic or resides near the shape's boundary, specifically in an area called $\widehat{\partial\Omega_\beta}$. This region is defined by taking points on the shape's boundary and moving them outward in an area that's both analytically and holomorphically solvable. We're discovering that any composition operator built from a function in this area will always be compact when it's mapping to or from an isometric state, with those isometries being either the constant one, $C_1$, or the original identity operator, $C_{\id}$. This discovery helps to extend earlier research that connected these operators to the underlying geometry of the space, specifically when it's both polydisc-like or convex and metrically smooth.

All-order results for the anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators derived from string theory are found to agree with the large-spin predictions from the Balitsky-Fermi-Virasoro (BFV) analysis, leading to further confirmation of the integrability-based technique for solving spectral problems with non-zero spin. Furthermore, this collaboration between world-sheet and world-volume methods has yielded simplified expressions for two-loop corrections in the spin expansion.

Dedicated GPU memory allocators have the potential to optimize memory access patterns 
and boost performance, but current solutions fail to accommodate application-specific 
dynamic memory requirements and often lead to underutilized GPU capacity due to 
fragmented memory usage. To overcome these limitations, we developed a novel memory 
allocator called Multi-dimensional Address-space Tailored Allocator for Ray-tracing on 
Accelerators (DynaSOAr), which seamlessly integrates with Kubernetes. DynaSOAr(Multi-dimensional Address-space Tailored Allocator for 
Ray-tracing on Accelerators) allows users to specify their application's memory 
needs through a YAML file, enabling efficient use of GPU capacity by shared memory. 
DynaSOAr showcases a 1.27X average speedup (up to 2.06X) in geometric ray-tracing 
algorithms by optimizing memory usage for user-defined addresses.

We investigate the possibility that Isospin Breaking exists between the proton and nucleus for dark matter particles that carry a charge under the U(1)_X gauge group. To comply with stringent constraints from direct detection experiments, we consider a scenario where Isospin Violation exists, allowing the dark matter particle to preferentially interact with the proton. This particle can then evade constraints from these experiments by significantly decreasing the cross-section with nuclei. Furthermore, we examine how relic abundance is affected by such a cross-section difference and find that under certain conditions, such cross-section variations can lead to the correct relic abundance. To validate our research, we focus on a specific mediator mass range that passes direct detection constraints, focusing on ultraviolet-sensitive annihilation processes that occur in the early universe. This involves considering three scenarios: (i) nucleon preference for a spin-0 or 3/2 target, (ii) a light medion, and (iii) Isospin Breaking with mediation by a nucleon-bound mediator. This last case allows for nuclei-favored cross-sections while adhering to direct detection constraints, offering new opportunities for a parameter of interest to slip through the cracks.

A crucial aspect of building straw tubes is ensuring they are pre-tensioned to an optimal level, which is directly related to their mechanical properties when in a vacuum. This is especially important for the XENONnT PMT wiring structure that uses straw tubes. An experiment was conducted where various manufacturers' straw tubes were tested using non-destructive methods in environments of both air and vacuum to identify their minimal pre-tension. The study found that the minimal pre-tension varies by straw tube manufacturer and that the preferred pre-tension should be within 10% above the minimum to maintain a stable high-voltage resistance in a vacuum.

The capacity to make decisions under uncertain conditions is a hallmark of the human ability to cope with uncertainty. We investigate how decision functions are maintained in the face of uncertain environmental conditions. To measure decision robustness, we employ a technique that utilizes optimal transport to calculate a minimum cost value transporter between training data distributions and potential testing data distributions. This approach allows us to measure the distance between training and potential testing data without assuming a parametric form for the data distribution. We measure the robustness of deep neural network-based classifiers by considering various potential data distribution shifts and measuring their impact on classification performance. The empirical analysis of the robustness of these classifiers reveals that they are generally not robust to distribution shifts. The analysis also shows a correlation between this lack of robustness and the complexity of the classifier. To address this issue, we utilize ensemble classifiers to improve the robustness of these models. The improved robustness of these models comes at a computational cost that must be balanced against the benefits of increased robustness. To mitigate this issue, we propose a technique that utilizes an uncertainty filter to decouple robustness from complexity in these models.

We investigate the impact of a time-periodic impurity on a supersolid under oscillatory driving. A quantum Monte Carlo simulation reveals that the impurity's motion influences the phonon spectrum, suppressing it at low frequencies, while enhancing it at high frequencies. Furthermore, continuous impurity movement eliminates the roton minimum and results in its transformation into an amplitude mode.

Unbiased transformations of coded geometric structures are known as neighbour-transitive codes. Currently, known instances of these codes, particularly within generalized quadrangles, predominantly originate from encoded symmetries of their point stabilizers. A comprehensive search for novel neighbour-transitive codes has yielded a complete list for generalized quadrangles, a result that also confirms the initial collection of these codes is exhaustive. Follow-up research revealed that an initial exhaustive collection of neighbour-orbits on line spreads also achieves this end for generalized quadrangles satisfying a specific geometric property.

The central region of the Milky Way holds immense significance for understanding galactic evolution and is home to a massive black hole at its core. Although the spatial distribution of the central molecular zone (CMZ) is symmetric, the gas velocity fields exhibit an asymmetry. To gain insight into the molecular gas dynamics, the angular momentum of the gas was analyzed. By doing so, the influence of density structure anisotropy, turbulent velocity anisotropy, and gravitational potential anisotropy on the gas angular momentum was determined. An ANISOFIT model was used to model the gravitational potential anisotropy, and an MCMC approach was used to find the optimal fit. Anisotropy maps were created for different scale ranges to study its dependence on anisotropy and the molecular gas dynamics. Our results indicate an anisotropy of 0.19 ± 0.01 in the 100-300 pc scale, decreasing with increasing Anisotropy length. Observations from the APEX telescope and MIRACLE instrument revealed a non-anisotropic distribution of the molecular gas in the 70 pc scale, but a significant anisotropy in the 300-1300 pc scale. Furthermore, an MCMC-based analysis revealed a turbulent anisotropy of 0.26 ± 0.02 in the 100-300 pc scale and a comparable

Our study examines the highly non-linear optical response of metallic nickel to intense laser fluences using a hybrid technique combining ablation threshold measurements and in-situ optical reflectivity analysis.  We found that while the laser pulse is absorbed linearly at lower fluences, non-linear absorption saturates and even declines at higher fluences.  This downwind change in absorption coincides with a substantial reduction in free electron density caused by high-electron speed collisions with the massive lattice.  Notably, we observed an ablation threshold rising with laser fluence, corresponding to the rising peak electron density.  Our findings demonstrate that the electron-based model can accurately predict the ablation threshold of metals under high-fluence conditions.

The objective of this study is to develop a non-invasive, real-time, non-contact temperature sensor that can accurately monitor skin surface temperature changes resulting from variations in ambient thermal conditions. By leveraging an LMGTO single photon detector and a Lock-in Amplifier, we demonstrate a novel ambient temperature sensing system, achieving a remarkable $0.015^\circ C$ resolution, outperforming standard temperature specifications by more than an order of magnitude. After conducting statistical analyses, we refine the system's accuracy to $0.02^\circ C$. Initial experiments are conducted to verify the system's capability to detect minute temperature fluctuations on the human skin surface.

Our proposal utilizes the quantum scissors technique to create highly entangled states of polarized photons on a large scale. We leverage both strong disperse properties of atoms and the quantum scissors method to produce multipartite entangled states, which can serve as the resource for measuring entanglement via correlation functions, facilitating the analysis of entangled photonic systems.

For a distance metric space consisting of n points and infinite-dimensional vector space, we define the online relative embeddability ratio $\rho_{\epsilon}$-approximate online d-spanner algorithms with p dimensions and real-valued metric as the smallest possible $\rho_{\epsilon}$ and the d-smallest online d-spanner algorithms. The algorithm must allow a small multiplicative distortion $\epsilon$ in the distance metric.

The analysis reveals that in higher-dimensional spaces with infinite points, $\rho_{\epsilon}$-approximate online d-spanner algorithms are not possible for any $d < d_{\epsilon}$, where $\epsilon$ depends on the specific algorithm's parameters.

However, we successfully designed an $\Ologd p\epsilon^{-2}$-approximate offline d-spanner algorithm in d dimensions with real-valued metric for any $d \geq 2$.

We also explored the possibility of $\rho_{\epsilon}$-approximate online d-spanner algorithms in the real-line metric space.

In this context, we found that for any $d \geq 2$, there exists a $\rho_{\epsilon}$-approximate online d-spanner algorithm in the real-line metric space with an infinite set of points.

Furthermore, we found that in the case of $d=1$, the only way to achieve a $\rho_{\epsilon}$-approximate online d-spanner algorithm in the real-line metric space is by using

This study investigates the effects of misidentifying IoT devices in learning cost. By treating errors as a statistical distribution, it reformulates classification problems in a likelihood framework and derives an optimal decision rule that balances accuracy and financial considerations. Contrary to existing research, this approach reframes cost as a metric related to classification mistakes, linking it to the concept of risk. Furthermore, it demonstrates that this rule can be expressed succinctely using the cost's derivative. Ultimately, this paper presents a novel risk measure tailored to IoT device classification and offers a simple, actionable method for its implementation.

There is a strong isomorphism between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, demonstrated through algebraic and combinatorial methods. This paper aims to demonstrate the fairness of this relationship by establishing a natural duality that links forests to Godel algebras. The study begins with an overview of fundamental concepts in duality theory for ordered structures, specifically a generalized dualization approach inspired by Priestley theory. Then, it shows that this approach can be applied to forests as partially ordered sets, and finally, it proves that finite Godel algebras are dual to finite forest sets, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between these mathematical structures.

Machine translation performance critically depends on the quality of alignment between source and target sentences. Although alignmenters like GIZA++ are routinely used, they have significant drawbacks, including high computational demands and the inflexibility to adapt to novel data without reprocessing previous alignments. In contrast, neural attention mechanisms used in current translation models can learn effective alignments alongside target translation, but these alignments are often inconsistent across models with different architectures or trained on varying corpora. In an effort to mitigate these issues, we introduce a deep learning approach for training alignmenters parametrically on relatively small corpora. The results of this investigation reveal that a deeply learned alignmenter trained solely on a 12MB corpus can process 16 million sentences per day and achieves alignment performance comparable to that of GIZA++. Furthermore, this developed aligner can enhance existing translations or models when used in combination. The developed alignmenter is available on GitHub for public use.

The paper introduces an asynchronous block-iterative decomposition algorithm with a general approach applicable across various iterative methods. This method leverages principles from Agrawal's asymptotic analysis but adapts it for iterative algorithms without regard to their specific type. Notably, the algorithm utilizes asynchronous updating within the context of its implementation.

This study aims to uncover the characteristics of black holes in the universe by conducting a thorough analysis of PBH events and comparing them to stellar-evolved black hole events. We utilize data from the EPOC survey, which monitors the OGLE-EPOC variable-source list by continuously observing the field in the direction of the Galactic center. Our analysis covers a three-year period (2017-2020) consisting of four-year intervals of observations. The results show that PBH events are anticipated to be more frequent than stellar-evolved black hole events by a factor of 33, assuming a certain mass distribution. Specifically, we expect around 0.33 events per year related to dark matter PBHs, with a probability range of 0.03 to 0.99, based on a specific mass distribution. Furthermore, PBH events are predicted to exhibit shorter caustic crossing durations than stellar-evolved black hole events. By analyzing the light curves of OGLE-EPOC-Ibn-7915, we identified a potential PBH event that exhibited a caustic radius similar to that of known relativistic images.

Due to its unique interplay of magnetic and structural factors, classifying frustrated materials is a complex and intriguing scientific challenge. At low packing densities, a model system of hard disks on a honeycomb lattice exhibits a polar ordered state, while at higher packing densities, a quasiperiodic tiling pattern emerges. However, through Monte Carlo simulations, polar ordered and quasiperiodic phases coexist beyond a packing density of 0.5, revealing lattice frustration at a packing density of 0.5 and introducing two novel phases - a polar ordered state with characteristic ferromagnetic ordering in all layers, and a quasiperiodic phase resembling a pinwheel quasicrystal. At packing densities greater than 0.5, the system also displays a one-quasiperiodic phase and exhibiting charge-density-wave-like behavior at specific cross sections.

This research examines how differentiation and integration affect zonal functions' positive definiteness. It has been discovered that specific differentiation and integration methods have positive definiteness-preserving properties. Consequently, this relationship has enabled positive definiteness to be used in deriving inequalities, such as the logarithmic Sobolev inequality, through a integration method. To generalize the integration process, a new integration operator has been created on the space of homogeneous polynomials, which also extends to all polynomials. Moreover, this newly created operator possesses a reproducing kernel property that was previously unrecognized.

The advanced technique of quantum imaging enables the detailed exploration of both invisible and highly sensitive samples. Interference patterns can be utilized to extract a variety of classical and quantum correlations, which serve as valuable resources in measurements and allow for the investigation of hidden objects through the effects of conditionals such as post-selection and quantum interference. Historically, interaction-free imaging has enabled the safe observation of delicate samples without direct interaction, which in turn has facilitated the development of high-precision quantum metrology. Building upon this foundation, our study extends existing concepts of quantum imaging to include the concept of interference of probabilities, which corresponds to the quantum information resource known as entanglement. This extension allows us to introduce a distinguished form of interaction-free imaging, which can be achievable even without delicate samples. As an application, we propose a quantum imaging technique that leverages the phenomenon of entanglement to perform image reconstruction. This proposed method not only enables the safe transmission of images but also opens the door to secure quantum communication that facilitates the delivery of complex visual content.

Researchers have been studying the ratchet effect in groups of people and various granular materials, but its existence in more fluid-based substances like expanded polystyrene and liquid soaps remains uncertain. In this review, we report the observation of the ratchet effect in the flow of pliable matter. Specifically, we report the flow rate of pliable matter through a series of increasingly larger openings, where the threshold opening size for the flow to initiate exhibits a size-based minimum. The size of these openings is defined by the height of the pliable material. The phenomenon can be attributed to the interaction between the pliable material's surface roughness, the flow's yield stress, and the size of the openings, where the surface roughness is defined as the height difference between the pliable material's peak and its base.

Deep learning-based computer vision technology has transformed the realm of image classification, facilitating widespread adoption in various applications. To further boost convolutional neural networks (CNNs) performance, researchers have explored multiple strategies, such as ensemble learning, which combines multiple models to enhance accuracy. This paper delves into a comprehensive comparison of modern general-purpose and CNN-specific generalization techniques, presenting a transparent, replicable approach called a transparency pipeline. Using three distinct image datasets - CIFAR10, ImageNet-SK, and TinyImageNet - we assess the effects of ensembling on a baseline network, along with a thorough analysis of the individual contributions of techniquies within the ensemble. The findings reveal that ensemble learning significantly boosts performance: CIFAR10 test accuracy enhancements of up to 0.5%, ImageNet-SK up to 3.0%, and a 4.0% improvement in Top-1 accuracy for TinyImageN. Notably, we discovered that FreeScale, an ensemble method, outperformed all others on both CIFAR10 and TinyImageNet. Furthermore, EnCNN, an method specifically designed for neural networks, demonstrated the highest accuracy gains on the ImageNet-SK dataset. By examining the ensemble pipeline, we identified a crucial role played by different freezing techniques in enhancing overall performance.

Researchers employed electron energy loss spectroscopy to examine dipolar electron-hole excitations in sodium, observing enhanced energy loss compared to standard electron-monopole electron-hloss spectroscopy. Through quantitative analysis, they determined the mass of dipolar excitations is approximately 1.26 times greater than that of monopole excitations, a value consistent with quantum mechanical predictions within experimental error margins. Furthermore, they found that dipolar excitations exhibit an increased screening charge of about 0.32 electrons relative to monopole excitations.

This note establishes a clear connection between dissipated work in thermodynamics and the concept of internal microwork performed by a specific state. It also provides a straightforward method for calculating the dissipated work value associated with any given state of a system that's gradually enlarged while maintaining specific constraints.

Cotangent bundle structures can be leveraged to simplify FLIPs into more manageable components, facilitating more in-depth analysis. This approach also enablesFLIPs related to section graphs to be expressed in terms ofFLIPs from the base manifold's boundary, thereby establishing key connections. Notably, this allows for a more comprehensive understanding of the curvature weights.

We continue our examination of the globally unstable behavior in finite diatomic chains based on Hertzian contact mechanics, building upon our prior research published in Nonlinearity in 2019. Our analysis reveals that two types of oscillations with extremely small amplitudes contribute to the formation of localized waves, despite the globally unstable nature of the system. These oscillations, specific to each unit within the spectrum, occur at distinct frequencies and give rise to spatially confined wave patterns. Their amplitudes are linked to the respective frequencies, resulting in two distinct regimes: one where the amplitude decay is linked to a specific eigenvalue, leading to faster localization, and another where the decay is linked to another eigenvalue, leading to slower localization. Our work also involves an in-depth examination of the associated eigenvalues and explores the connection between them.

The focus is on a class of inflation models with sharp features in the inflaton potential, which can produce distinct signatures in primordial non-Gaussianities (NGs), even when the slow-roll approximation holds. We investigate multiple cases of the inflaton field's initial and intermediate dynamics, including resonant particle production during a transient violation of the slow-roll conditions. Our analysis indicates that the non-Gaussianity signal generated by a short slow-roll phase can be significantly larger than that produced by a prolonged slow-roll phase or by a standard single-field inflation. We also explore how an additional scalar field can interact with the inflaton during the short slow-roll phase, leading to the production of non-Gaussianities on large scales. Numerical simulations demonstrate that these signals are robust against potential non-adiabatic sources of non-Gaussianity, such as quantum fluctuations or mode interactions.

The accordion graph class $I[n,k]$ was studied, but a different notation is used here. For instances where $4 \leq k \leq n-1$, we determine the exact graph isomorphism complexity. When the parameter $k$ falls within the range $4 \leq k \leq n-1$, we identify the conditions under which $I[n,k]$ is a circulant graph. For certain values of $k$, specifically $4 \leq k \leq n-1$, we fully characterize the commutative Cayley graphs within this graph class. Furthermore, for the specific cases where $n=2^m$ and $k=2^m+3$, we prove that every graph in $I[2^m, 2^m+3)$ can be represented as a circulant graph. We also establish a comprehensive characterization of the symmetric difference between any two distinct graphs in $I[n,k]$. Building upon this foundation, we develop a polynomial-time algorithm to establish graph isomorphism for the accordion graph class.

In this study, we examine the temporal evolution of the participation ratio in a one-dimensional non-ergodic quantum walk near a detrapping angle. By conducting numerical simulations, we discovered that the participation ratio exhibits a power-law behavior, following $P(t) \propto t^{\beta}$, where the exponent $\beta$ varies depending on the detrapping angle. Notably, we observed that the participation ratio is influenced by the initial coin state but remains unaffected by the initial state of the walker.

Recent findings from the self-supervised field have revealed that fully-convolutional methods like DINO can match or surpass heavily-supervised models on specific tasks, while also providing a strong foundation for transfer learning. This study investigates the effect of weakly-supervised pre-training on learning visual representations using Transformers. We found that using DINO to pre-train Transformers is a valuable strategy in improving their performance. Moreover, by analyzing the dynamics within the model, we discovered that each Transformer module has the capacity to learn complex representations independently. This is further validated by observing the behavior of neural gradients and convergence rates across different layers during training. As a result, using smaller and more computationally efficient models is possible without compromising the quality of the final representation. Based on these insights, we created new, lightweight ViT models that consistently produce superior representations. On the challenging ImageNet benchmark, our smallest model is actually stronger than the original, largest and most computationally expensive model. These results have also been replicated using ResNet as a backbone. All code and experimental setups are publicly available.

A purely gravitational, higher-order viscosity model is proposed, extending from earlier research on relativistic cosmology with a dynamical, symmetric tensor viscosity coefficient. This new model, rooted in the Einstein field equations, introduces a single scalar function for the dynamic viscosity coefficient, $f(t)$, and explores its implications in a radiating universe scenario. By integrating a few reasonable assumptions, the study re-examines key cosmological parameters, revealing that the dynamic viscosity's evolution aligns with the universe's expansion, energy loss, and temperature changes, all consistent with a fluid cooling effect. Additionally, the study validates its predictions through data from supernovae, the cosmic microwave background, and the Hubble parameter, showing that a gradually increasing dynamic viscosity, starting at a quantified value, provides a satisfactory explanation for the accelerated universe expansion.

The Cauchy problem for incompressible Euler equations exhibits well-posedness in dimensions up to four, but we demonstrate that it's extremely ill-posed with smooth data in dimensions five or higher, regardless of the smoothness of the vector field, due to a mechanism akin to the resonant bootstrap process in wave maps equations. 
Specifically, we show that the Euler equations map $C^\infty$ functions to $C^{N-11}$ functions for any $N$, and through iterative application, we can show that given any target smoothness level, we can repeatedly iterate until we reach a space where the solution becomes well-posed, leading to an arbitrary degree of smoothness loss, a phenomenon referred to as the smoothness trap. 
We leverage this to establish a universal smoothness trap across various PDEs, providing an upper bound for the maximal degree of smoothness in each case, a key component of the backreaction mechanism responsible for irregularity in long-wave dynamics.

Artificial intelligence technologies enable users to swiftly create customized images based on their unique preferences. Nevertheless, collaborating with humans on this process remains challenging due to the intricate and multifaceted nature of controlling a computer's artistic creative process. Existing tools either necessitate extensive programming knowledge or require users to manually create lengthy text prompts. To tackle this problem, we introduce Stable Artist, a novel system that empowers users to refine and customize the process of generating images using artificial intelligence. By integrating interactive design patterns, machine learning, and the latest advancements in the implicit graph representation of image generation processes, users can control the creative process at multiple levels of detail, from macro artistic choices to fine-grained adjustments. Furthermore, users can save and save their artistic styles and compositions for later use, and collaborate effectively across various platforms. By enabling users to collaborate and save their compositions, Stable Artist empowers users to control the computer's artistic creative process with greater flexibility and control.

Deep learning's appeal lies in its ability to deliver impressive predictions, yet its complexity often obscures these algorithms from the lens of probabilistic modeling. Despite advances, accurately measuring the uncertainty of these models remains a pressing issue. We present a method for quantifying the reliability of trained deep neural networks by leveraging the Kullback-Leibler divergence and extending Koenig and Sudderth's work on distribution comparison. Furthermore, our approach incorporates the concept of effective components from Sudderth and Kirkner's research on variational Bayes. The result is a single score that can measure the predictive accuracy of a neural network and the complexity of its learned distribution. The complexity score can also serve as a proxy for the reliability score in scenarios where access to test data is limited. The proposed framework has been implemented using a simple feed-forward neural network and demonstrated through simulation studies on a diagonal covariance learning problem.

New constraints on a spin-0 dark matter particle interacting with non-dark matter particles are imposed, considering both nucleon and nucleus-mediated scatterings, alongside a specific decay of the $J/\psi$ particle into invisible particles. Experimental data from the FNAL/E871 and LHCb experiments are analyzed to derive these constraints, which are then compared with the theoretical predictions based on the simplest model of four scalar particles. These considerations lead to impactful limitations on dark matter-nucleon scatterings, which are significant across a broad range of masses for the dark matter particle. Ultimately, the analysis of these constraints provides a comprehensive link between dark matter interactions and the standard model of particle physics.

A comprehensive analysis of magnetic bright points has been conducted,
involving observations from the SDO/AIA and IRIS instruments. The focus
is on examining velocity field components and their behavior over time.
The study collected samples from multiple magnetic bright points and
analyzed the motion along three velocity vector components.
Statistical tests revealed that the movement in all three directions
follows a Gaussian pattern, with the highest average speed occurring along
the field line. Moreover, the average motion in the two components
perpendicular to the field is found to be S-ward. This motion is
attributed to a significant S-wind. The observed effects of the wind are
also found to influence both the cross-spectral analysis and the energy
balance within these magnetic bright points.

The individual experiencing vision loss due to eye disease often struggles to make sense of the world, yet remains unable to share their impaired vision with others. To explore how subtle changes in human dynamic vision affect vision recognition, our study utilizes minimal videos featuring human actions to assess the robustness of deep learning models for human action recognition across a range of vision simulations. Inspired by the principles of empathy, our work seeks to contribute toward developing adaptive robotic assistance for individuals with eye disease by first understanding the impact of compromised vision on vision recognition, thereby laying the groundwork for a potential solution. To simulate vision impairment, our study applies a parametric approach, modifying key aspects of vision such as contrast, color, and clarity in a gradual manner. Initially, our study simulates common distortions found in the general population, such as age-related changes and common genetic conditions like Cystic Chorioretinopathy. Subsequently, our study gradually transforms healthy vision simulations into severe vision loss simulations, ultimately reaching the extreme end of impairment.

We've used the functional approach to study bound monopoles in a three-dimensional SU(2) gauge theory with a compact dimension. By introducing an external magnetic field along the x3 axis, we found that bound monopole ground states are significantly impacted, even without quantum corrections. Our findings suggest that the magnetic field binds the monopole-antimonopole system more tightly, while the excited states show a 'quasi-dissociation' as a result of the magnetic field. Ultimately, we derived an explicit expression for the monopole's mass within an external magnetic field.

Deep learning based weather forecasting models have gained significant traction in recent years. Despite initial reports comparing their accuracy to traditional statistical methods, further investigation was warranted due to the lack of detailed analysis surrounding these results. We assessed two weather forecasting models utilizing three different statistical metrics and found that normalizing the dataset led forecasting models to surpass statistical models in accuracy by around 15%. Furthermore, we discovered that statistical metrics had varying sensitivities to statistical distributions, and that dataset size played a crucial role in evaluating forecasting models. Our findings emphasize the necessity of dataset preparation and assessment in forecasting model evaluations. Our analysis is accessible on our website at https://meteoschool.github.io/deep-vs-physics/.

In models involving multiple dark matter candidates, understanding their interaction with each other is crucial for determining the efficiency of their scattering processes and thus their space density. This study investigates dark matter interactions in two-specific three-Higgs-doublet models with varying numbers of CP-violating sources. Even with a single source of CP-violation, these models' dark matter regions of interaction are substantial. Furthermore, their multi-component nature leads to several areas where the dark matter candidates' masses can coexist. This research also highlights the model parameters' sensitivity in influencing the phase space of dark matter mass combinations and concludes that their interconnectedness renders these models fine-tuned.

Our theory's development continues as we explore its applications to other areas. A key point of consideration involves the PPT square conjecture, which can be analyzed through a specific transformation related to the problem at hand. Furthermore, we demonstrate that concepts from the PPT square conjecture can be mapped onto our framework for entanglement detection in its simplest case. Additionally, we show that the element corresponding to a pure state has a property confirming the conjecture through a detailed analysis using the diagonalisation method.

The efficient delivery of essential cargo to distal brain regions relies on a precise molecular transport system that operates along the framework provided by microtubules and their organizing proteins. To gain a deeper understanding of the structural and chemical properties of microtubules in relation to transport, researchers developed a computational model that incorporates a variety of geometric factors such as helical alignment of microtubule strands and cross-sectional profiles. The results of the study show that helical geometry can lead to the formation of complex three-dimensional transport paths, but that these effects can be mitigated through the proper alignment of molecular motors. The study's findings also highlight the significance of considering cross-sectional variations in microtubule structure in addition to traditional linear models. The outcomes of this research provide valuable insights into how neural networks function at a systems level, helping to clarify the relationship between microtubule structure and the spread of excitatory signals in the form of calcium waves within the brain. The insights gained from this work can serve as a foundation for exploring the role of diffusive and molecular transport processes in other complex biological systems, offering a potential pathway to further our comprehension of brain function and learning.

In recent years, graph learning techniques have gained significant attention in the realm of graph machine learning, particularly in the area of online banking fraud detection. Most existing approaches rely on historical transaction data to construct graphs for modeling. However, due to the complex nature of actual banking transactions, learned models based on real data often struggle to generalize when applied to different scenarios. To overcome this limitation, this research introduces a novel approach called progressive graph learning, which starts with simple rules to construct initial graphs and gradually incorporates historical transactions to refine and improve the graph model. This innovative method not only enables the creation of empty graph samples essential for training but also facilitates the development of more accurate and complex banking graphs that accurately represent various transaction patterns. Our experiments using a real-world online banking dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, showcasing its ability to accurately detect fraud in various banking scenarios and achieve top-tier performance in existing fraud detection benchmarks. The source code will be made publicly available.

Mass transfer from a white dwarf star losing mass at a rate of $\sim10^{-7}M_{\odot}$/yr can initiate the formation of a black hole acccretion disc following stellar mergers such as mergers between a novae star and a neutron star.  This allows for the exploration of whether these discs will emit detectable radio signals at frequencies of $\geq1$GHz. Calculations indicate a connection between the distance of the emitting black hole and the angle at which radio waves reach an observer, resulting in a characteristic curved pattern in radio sky maps. Curved patterns of radio signal intensity are expected around every second black hole in the galaxy due to their alignment with the velocity of stellar objects in the galaxy's disk. The most prominent signals may be produced in the early stages of a white dwarf star's evolution due to the higher likelihood of star formation in the galaxy's inner regions with shorter wavelengths of radio waves having greater sensitivity to closer objects in the galaxy's center.

The study of CP violations in processes involving the coherent phase space of three-body semileptonic tau decays could offer a promising avenue for exploring CP violation in the complete sector of quark and lepton flavor. To achieve this, we need to study tau couplings to new bosons and the properties of newly discovered resonances, such as their masses and coupling constants with the standard model electroweak bosons and quarks. These studies can be carried out at a future lepton collider, such as a linear e+e- collider with center-of-mass energy of 250 GeV or 500 GeV. It is also possible to perform these studies at hadron colliders like the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) with high luminosity, providing complementary information to our understanding of new physics.

We identify the boundary or extremal points of a specific set of psychometrically significant metric spaces, derived from the symmetric Tversby ratio models. The embedded metric spaces are uniformly populated with their extreme points, which correspond to well-known similarity structures. The method for finding these extreme points involves solving an associated optimization issue, and it is also shown that the entire set of such metrics is a convex set.

This work presents a novel, highly task-oriented computer vision framework for deconvolution-based deblurring network training. Unlike conventional methods that rely on empirical atomic point targets, our framework leverages high-quality synthetic training samples to accelerate the development of atomic point deconvolution networks. To mimic real-world image blurring effects and produce diverse training samples, our framework incorporates a dynamic 'reblurring module'. This module enhances network learning capacity and accelerates its convergence. Moreover, our framework utilizes atomic point-based residual learning within deblurring networks to minimize point target reliance. We have implemented this framework specifically for SRDeblur, a recent SRDeblurring solution. Experimental results confirm that the SRDeblur model trained with our method surpasses models trained on atomic point targets when paired for the super-resolution deblurring and blurring tasks.

Recent discoveries in neuroscience and machine learning have revealed parallels between learning processes in simple chemical reaction networks (CRNs) and in artificial neural networks. The current research explores whether a chemical basis for autonomous learning, analogous to that in a learning neuron, can be found by mapping artificial neural networks to reaction networks. A comprehensive modeling framework is proposed to represent membrane potential as a species in CRNs, capturing both passive membrane dynamics and the active all-or-none action potential behavior, which is found to correspond to a type of autonomous learning in CRNs. The dynamics of CRNs are then analyzed through specific example cases.

We investigate the concept of open completeness in comparison with strong open completeness for continuous open semantics. It is established that strong open completeness implies open completeness, though not vice versa, with this relationship dependent on the original set's density. We introduce an expanded universe construction that ensures any dense set has a strong open complete ultrapower, using the same ultrafilter. Additionally, we prove that any universe can be widened to a dense set, which when ultrafiltered, yields a strong open complete ultrapower, used as an intermediate step in the proof.

In the era of data-driven science, benchmarking is now essential for the fair comparison of solutions and promotes transparency and reproducibility. Nevertheless, benchmarking large datasets can be a resource-intensive process, restricting the availability of existing benchmarks to a smaller group of researchers with high-performance computing access. To tackle this challenge, we propose a process for pre-computing benchmark suites during benchmark creation, ensuring that accuracy is maintained through an error estimation framework. We also present a publicly accessible repository that facilitates the distribution of benchmark datasets, accommodating various high-performance computing environments and taking into consideration quantum-boosting techniques for accelerated benchmarking. By implementing these strategies, we have successfully increased the range of users who can utilize our benchmark from 45 to 261, allowing for benchmarking even the most complex simulations with just a minute-long computation time.

Chen, K., Rood, D., and Wang, X. previously demonstrated that for any positive integer $t$, there exists a graph which contains $t$-coloring but no $K_t$-minor, yet is three-connected and devoid of any $\sqrt t$-coloring. Our current work expands on their findings by providing a $\log t$-coloring restriction for the aforementioned class of graphs.

The performance of an adaptive cost function, which adjusts its parameters in response to varying input conditions, is heavily influenced by its ability to efficiently track the optimal set of parameters in real-time. Research into this topic typically assumes a pre-defined cost function structure, which either utilizes input data or transforms it before optimization. A single-layer transformation results in a straightforward relationship between the input and optimal parameters, whereas multi-layer transformations result in a complex, non-convex relationship that hinders efficient optimization. This paper introduces a novel cost function, the convex mirror algorithm, which utilizes a specific function to maintain a convex relationship between optimized parameters and input data, thereby enabling real-time optimization. The study evaluates the impact of this cost function on various inputs and compares its efficiency to alternative approaches, including regularization methods. Results indicate that the proposed cost function generally achieves optimal results within a fraction of the total available time, although its performance can be sensitive to the choice of parameters.

To effectively utilize entangling collisions for quantum metrology, the first
step is to produce atom-atom entangling collisions in a controlled and random
manner reminiscent of a Poisson process, thus generating an atomic state analogous
to a temporal cluster state, enabling efficient exploitation of quantum resources
in quantum metrology, as previously explored in studies on entangling collisions.
The current investigation delves into the effects of different triggering methods
on the atom-atom entangling collisions in a two-species atomic sample, revealing
varying degrees of entanglement and entanglement structure for a specific
two-dimensional entanglement measure in angle space. Furthermore, the study offers
two distinct triggering techniques and evaluates their effect on the sensitivity of
the atomic state in quantum metrology, showing that a controlled and deterministic
triggering strategy yields the highest sensitivity, while random triggering falls
somewhere in between the purely deterministic and random strategies.
